speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have an inquiry which I should like to direct to the Minister of Labour. Will he be good enough to give a full statement to the house with respect to the strike of the employees of the Montreal Tramways company, so that hon. members may have full information?

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it
might be just as well, in view of the inquiry of my hon. friend, to place on the record definite particulars in regard to this matter.
There is an agreement between the company and its emploj'ees which was entered into in July of 1940. The agreement was consummated between the company and a negotiating committee representing the employees. Clause 109 of that agreement reads as follows:
The negotiating committee referred to in this agreement, consisting of Messrs. Elphege Beaudoin, Raoul Trepanier and Osias Neveu, will continue in office during the life of the agreement.
The members of the committee were all officers of local 780 of the Amalgamated Association of Electric Railways and Motor Coach Employees of America.
At the time the agreement was made it can be assumed that the majority of the employees were members of this union because the agreement was confirmed by a majority vote of the employees at that time.
Subsequently another labour organization, the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees and other transport workers, entered the field and began to organize the employees of the company, and on March 2, 1943. sub-

Montreal Tramways Strike
mitted to the Department of Labour an application for the establishment of a board of conciliation and investigation under the pro-visons of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
It was set out in the application that the cause of the dispute was the claim of employees to be represented by the person or persons of their choice and that such request had been refused by the company.
Following the usual practice an industrial disputes inquiry commissioner was authorized to investigate the nature and cause of the dispute with a view to adjusting it. All the interested parties made representations to the commissioner, including members of the negotiating committee, officers of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees and other transport workers, representatives of the Catholic syndicate and the assistant general manager of the company. While the report of the commission was before the department for consideration it appears that the negotiating committee requested permission of the company to take a vote on the premises of the company, which permission was granted by the company. This negotiating committee, of course, were members of the amalgamated association of street railway electrical employees. The ballot to read as follows:
The National War Labour Board has just been changed. This change gives the negotiating committee the opportunity to make new attempts with regard to wages. Are you in favour of according the negotiating committee all the support it will need to undertake these attempts on your behalf?
Thereupon the company was advised by the representatives of the employees who were members of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, and other transport workers, that if such ballot were held, all employees, members of the brotherhood, would cease work on Monday, March 29.
So much for the background of this strike. The contract made between the company and its employees was made for a period of three years or for the duration of the war, whichever was the longer. No doubt the company thought its labour relations were settled for the duration; however, the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees quite evidently have enlisted the affiliation of, if not a majority of the employees, certainly a very large proportion of them. This is evidenced by the fact that the strike has taken place. The hon. gentlemen will note that the contract covered a considerable period of time.
The threat of a stoppage of work was made known to officials of the department on Saturday, March 27, and was confirmed in a telegram from Mr. D. E. Blair, General Manager
of Montreal Tramways company, to me which was received late last Saturday evening.
Saturday and Sunday were devoted to efforts to reach an understanding which would provide for settlement of the dispute. On Sunday, March 28, I sent telegrams and in order that they may be on record, I am going to read the telegram sent to Mr. Blair:
March 28, 1943.
Mr. D. E. Blair,
Vice President and General Manager,
Montreal Tramways Co., Montreal, Quebec.
Replying your telegram twenty-seventh regarding possibility of strike employees your company occurring to-morrow morning, in view of serious nature of situation it is my intention to establish at once a commission or board of conciliation and investigation with a view to conciliation of the existing dispute. It would appear however that if a stoppage of work tomorrow morning and consequent disruption of traffic is to be avoided company should postpone decision on request of negotiating committee for ballot to be taken to-morrow on company premises. Please let me have your decision on this point by seven p.m. to-day in order that departmental officers may communicate with all parties claiming to represent employees.
Humphrey Mitchell.
I also wired the representatives of the unions concerned as follows:
Mr. A. R. Mosher.
President C.B.R.E. & O.T.W.,	.
230 Laurier Ave. West,
Ottawa.
In connection with letter received yesterday by Mr. D. E. Blair General Manager Montreal Tramways Company signed by Presidents locals 210, 214 and 219 of your organization and your own telegram to him of March 27 relative to strike action to-morrow of members of above locals in protest against ballot proposed to be taken by presently recognized negotiating committee, I have decided in view of serious effects of any disruption of Montreal tramways or bus services to appoint a commission or board of conciliation at once with view to conciliation of existing dispute. In meantime desire to warn you that strike of employees of company members locals your organization referred to above would be illegal and you are urged to take necessary steps to prevent the action contemplated by them.
Humphrey Mitchell,
Minister of Labour.
Mr. Elphege Beaudoin,
Business Agent,
Union D'Employ de Tramways de Montreal,
1153 St. Denis, Montreal.
Have received telegram from D E Blair General Manager Montreal Tramways Company relative to threatened strike of certain employees of the company members of three locals of Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees and other transport workers in protest against proposed ballot to be taken to-morrow among all employees of the company by your negotiating committee with permission of company management. In view of serious disruption of tramway and bus services in Montreal which will ensue from strike of any substantial number
Montreal Tramways Strike

of employees of company I have decided to establish at once a commission or board of conciliation to endeavour to conciliate the dispute. Urge your committee in meantime to postpone proposed ballot and let all matters come before this tribunal. Such postponement will not in my opinion prejudice the interests of membership your organization. Hope you can give me an affirmative reply this evening.
Humphrey Mitchell.
To these telegrams the following replies were received:
Hon. Humphrey Mitchell,
Ministry of Labour, Ottawa.
Your telegram has received our careful consideration. As we have indicated we granted permission to the negotiating committee to hold ballot and we do not see our way clear to withdraw permission except on their request. Have spoken to Mr. Beaudoin who refuses to postpone ballot.
D. E. Blair.
Hon. Humphrey Mitchell,
Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
A stoppage of work by employees of Montreal Tramways Company will be as unwelcome by me as anyone. If the government with the authority it has cannot restrain the company from collaborating with those seeking to place its employees in an untenable position it is unreasonable to expect me with the limited authority I have to prevent employees from refusing to report for duty.
A. R. Mosher.
Hon. Humphrey Mitchell,
Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
Postpone ballot only moderate routine. Our members will not stop work. CBRE should be made to understand that this is no reason for a strike. Our local established in Montreal since nineteen eighteen and intends to stay. Executive meeting presently and will take decision during the night.
Elphege Beaudoin,
President Local 790.
As everyone knows, the strike occurred on Monday morning, March 29, and the situation is very serious, mainly because important war productions are seriously handicapped because men cannot get to work.
This condition cannot be permitted to continue. I have already sent Doctor H. C. Goldenberg to Montreal as commissioner under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act to see if he can bring the parties together. I selected him because he was born in Montreal, is bilingual, and an important officer of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which department is vitally interested in this dispute. Doctor Goldenberg is in a position to make strong representations on behalf of both departments. He has had a great deal of experience in matters of this kind.
I feel quite confident that the better judgment of both the management and the men will prevail and that the men will be back to work very shortly.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley for committee of supply.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a discussion of the government's grain marketing policy is long overdue in this house. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) made a statement on January 29 regarding the government's grain marketing policy for disposing of the 1943-44 crop. This is the only statement that has been made, and from that time until now no opportunity has been presented to hon. members to offer suggestions or to enter into any discussion with reference to this policy. Therefore I think that the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has rendered a real service by bringing up this matter and placing it before the house.
A habit has developed in this house of having ministers of the crown make important statements of policy on the orders of the day. There is then no opportunity for discussing them or for asking questions, and above all there is no opportunity to offer constructive suggestions. It seems to me that this house should not only assent to, or dissent from, legislation; one of our functions should be to make suggestions as to how legislation can be improved and to inform ministers how any particular piece of legislation will affect the constituents whom we represent. That has not been done. Again and again hon. members are being presented with a fait accompli. We are told, " Here is the policy; take it or leave it."
Once or twice the hon. member for Melfort tried to get some statement from the minister to the effect that the grain marketing policy of the government would be referred to the agriculture committee. The minister agreed to this, but so far the policy has not been submitted to the agriculture committee, and there has been no opportunity for discussing it. If it serves no other purpose than to have brought about this discussion in the house and to have elicited statements from responsible ministers, the debate will have been worth while.
Not only has parliament been ignored in this matter; organized agriculture has been almost completely ignored. When the minister made his statement on January 29 he said that there had been conferences with various bodies, and he included among them the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We
were all a little surprised when some of the officials of that organization at a meeting in Calgary appeared to be quite indignant and said that they had not been consulted. We begin to see now why they were indignant. Since that time the brief which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, presented to the government on January 19, has been made public. This brief was presented to the government ten days before the minister made his statement in this house. Nine points were submitted to the government, and the government has completely ignored them all with the exception of one. Submission No. 1 in the brief submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asked for an initial price of SI per bushel, basis Fort William. This was ignored. No. 2 asked for a domestic price of SI .35 per bushel. Ignored. No. 3 asked that there should be no reduction in the total deliverable quantity of wheat in the coming year and that farmers should be allowed to deliver grain of the 1942 crop year on the 1943 quota. This submission and this alone was accepted by the government. No. 4 asked the government to pay storage on the deliverable portion of a farmer's grain. Also ignored. No. 5 asked that the guaranteed price for flax should be increased from $2.25 to $2.50 per bushel. This also was completely ignored. No. 6 asked for a system of advances to be paid on that quantity of the farmer's crop which he must hold until the government has sufficient facilities to take care of it. This too has been ignored. No. 7 asked for a comprehensive soil survey. No. S asked for $4 an acre to be paid on land taken out of cultivation and seeded to grass. This too was rejected. No. 9 asked that the Canadian wheat board be authorized to handle coarse grains on the same basis as wheat is now being handled by that board. This also has been completely overlooked.
Here is a marketing policy brought down by the government on the opening day of this session, a policy which neither the house nor any committee of the house has had an opportunity to discuss. Of the nine recommendations made by the leading organized agriculture body of Canada only part of one of the nine has been accepted by the government. Therefore I think it is high time that private members of this house took the only opportunity which presents itself, namely, on the motion to go into supply, of asking for a full discussion of the policy and for a statement from the minister.
I want to cite five things about this policy. First, the grain marketing policy outlined by the minister on January 29 and carried on by the government for the last eight years has been a policy which deliberately sought to

Western Grain Crop

sabotage and discredit the wheat board in the eyes of the wheat producers of western Canada. The Liberal party never wanted a wheat board. They opposed the legislation in 1934 and 1935. They opposed the compulsory features of it. They were responsible for having put back into it the operation of the open market and the continuance of the Winnipeg grain exchange in our grain economy. When they were elected in 1935 they began the long process, which is still continuing, of discrediting and sabotaging the wheat board. One of the first things done was to appoint new personnel. The chairman appointed at that time was Mr. J. R. Murray, the former secretary of the Winnipeg grain exchange and one of the men who had led the lobby against the wheat board act when it was being passed by parliament the year before. I said in this house at the time, in 1936, that putting Mr. Murray in charge of the wheat board was like putting a skunk in the henhouse to raise chickens, and I have never had any reason to revise my judgment in that matter.
What happened? In 1936 one of the first things done was to say that the farmers could not deliver their wheat to the wheat board even if they wanted toas long as the price of wheat stayed above ninety cents a bushel the farmer had to sell his wheat on the open market. Every hon. member from western Canada knows what the result was. What happened was that in the fall of 1936-because that policy stayed in operation for two years- farmers sold their wheat at a price basis Fort William varying between ninety cents and $1 a bushel. The next spring wheat was selling on the Winnipeg grain exchange at as high as $1.47 and $1.48 a bushel. Who made the difference, the spread between what the farmer sold at in the fall of 1936 and the price in the open market in the spring of 1937? The speculators made it. We had the bitter spectacle of the farmers having seed grain advanced to them through this government and the provincial governments, for which they signed notes at SI.45 a bushel-for seed wheat much of which had been bought on the prairies at less than a dollar a bushel the previous year.
In other words the policy with reference to the wheat board seems to have been that on a falling market the wheat board will be rushed in to carry the load, while on a rising market the speculator will be allowed to come in and reap his gain at the expense of the farmer.
In 1940 once more the price was up above the price which the farmer was receiving. At that time we had a general election. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will remember that the statement was made frequently during that election-
'Mr. T. C. Douglas.]

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I heard that speech you are now making during that campaign.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is just as true now as it was then. The statement was made then by the Minister of Agriculture and others that because the price that was being paid for the farmer's wheat was considerably higher than the farmer was getting, there would be something payable on his participation certificates. He was getting seventy cents a bushel. The Regina Leader-Post of February 9, 1940, said:
Canadian farmers who delivered wheat to the wheat board, under present price conditions should receive from five to eight cents a bushel for their wheat for participation certificates, with chances of better prices yet prevailing, Hon, J. G. Gardiner, federal minister of agriculture, told an audience of nearly 700 people here Thursday night.
Sale of wheat now held by the board at a price between 82 and 85 cents should make such a further payment possible providing storage charges and other costs can be avoided, he said.
Hundreds of farmers across the prairies hold these participation certificates, and to every farmer they are a mute reminder of the failure of the government to make good that promise. But worse; it makes the farmer feel that these pieces of paper are worthless, consequently that orderly marketing is worthless and that the wheat board is worthless, because, those who sold on the open market got a better return than they did. The net result in the long run will be that unless this policy is changed the farmers who were most anxious to have a wheat board are going to lose faith in the board. That is why I say that if this government had deliberately set out to sabotage and discredit the wheat board they could not have done a better job than has been done by the programme that they have followed over these years.
Now we come to the present situation. The Minister of Agriculture did not hear this in 1940. The situation to-day is, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Melfort yesterday, that wheat and coarse grains are higher on the open market than the price the farmer is receiving through the board. Secondly, the price of wheat and coarse grains in the United States is much higher than the price on the open market in Canada. Who is getting the benefit of the spread between the price on the open market and the price which the farmer receives from the board? There is an 11-cent spread at the present moment on No. 1 wheat; it is SI-01 in the open market and 90 cents on sales to the board. I have here a list of the spreads in the different grades as of March 11 last, varying all the way from 6} cents to 16J cents, while on the tough grades the spread varies all the way from cents to 18J cents.

Western Grain Crop
Who is getting the benefit of that? Is the farmer getting the benefit of that spread? He is not, if we can believe the reports that are coming from the west. I have here a clipping from the Regina Leader-Post, of a dispatch from Winnipeg dated March 12, which says:
Western farmers will shortly be given an opportunity to take advantage of the recent aggressive advance in Winnipeg wheat prices, it was indicated in the grain trade here Friday.
While George Mclvor, chairman of the wheat board, is in Ottawa conferring with government officials, it is known that line elevator association officials had conferences with him on the price situation before his departure. It is understood that the line elevators have worked out a plan and will issue a price list based on open market quotations at an early date. The elevator companies have had to deal with war shipping delays and a shortage of railway equipment, which interfered with normal hedging operations.
From Ottawa it was reported that while wheat prices are running above the wheat board price, farmers could take advantage of this rise on the open market if the elevator company could obtain insurance against shipping delays. There has been an acute shortage of grain cars, and naturally the elevator companies are unable to pay the higher prices if they cannot be sure of cars in which to ship the wheat thus sold.
There is, apparently, a demand in the west that the wheat board should provide guarantees against shipping delays, but inquiry here reveals little support for such a solution. The government, however, has been making extraordinary efforts to obtain more cars, and it is thought the situation will improve steadily. As more cars became available the need of insurance against shipping delays would diminish.
What has been happening? The average line elevator company is not prepared to accept delivery of wheat at the open market price unless it can be sure of shipping it out immediately. Therefore, if he cannot get cars, the farmer must sell to the wheat board at 90 cents. Who gets the benefit of the SI .01 in the open market? For a considerable time now the wheat board has been selling wheat at the head of the lakes to commission men and speculators. These firms now have large surpluses of wheat. They are the people who have the wheat on hand and are able to take advantage of the open market. The farmer cannot take advantage of it unless he can. get cars. I believe the people on the grain exchange who bought this wheat for much less than it is worth to-day are the people who can take advantage of the open market; and they are the people who are getting any benefit that is accruing out of this increased) price in the open market.
Again I would ask, who is getting the advantage of the difference between the Winnipeg open market price and the United States market price? Once more it is not the farmer. A return already has been brought down
72537-108}
showing the number of permits granted for the export of coarse grains. We have not yet received a list of the permits granted for the export of wheat, but I imagine we shall get it in time. Why is not the wheat board exporting wheat and coarse grains? Why is it not carrying on these negotiations and sales, in order to ensure that all the money received for the wheat and coarse grains will go back to the farmers who grew them? Instead I believe the people who stand to benefit by the spread between Canadian and United States market prices are the exporters and commission men, the people who speculate in foodstuffs, in the sweat and toil of the prairie farmer. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. Surely in war time this government and this parliament is not going to allow any group of people to speculate, to gamble or to profiteer in the foodstuffs that are so essential for the winning of the war, or upon the livelihood of the people who work on the farms of this country.
Therefore, sir, before going on with the remainder of what I have to say, I want to move, seconded by the hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. Wright):
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"This house desires to record its opinion that the grain marketing policy of the government is detrimental to the public interest and that steps should be taken to abolish trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange, in order to prevent speculation and profiteering at the expense of the farmer."
Following, that amendment I want to suggest that the government, through the wheat board, should accept delivery of coarse grains in the same manner that they have been accepting delivery of wheat; and that instead of turning these grains over to speculators, commission men and exporters when they reach the head of the lakes, the wheat board should not only accept delivery of the wheat and coarse grains but should also accept responsibility for the negotiations preceding sale, and the sale of these commodities. If that were done the farmer would be sure that every cent coming from the sale of these products would be returned to him. He would know that no one was speculating, that no one was getting a slice out of his share, somewhere between him and the ultimate consumer. That would mean that the wheat board would have to pay a fair and reasonable price for these commodities; and it is certain that at the present time, as shown by the open market prices in Canada, in the United States and in Great Britain, the farmer is not receiving a reasonable price. He is receiving a price that is far below parity, even for coarse grains, in spite of the fact that the Minister
Western Grain Crop

of Agriculture stated that coarse grains were the limiting factor upon how much live stock we could produce in this country.
The impression sometimes goes out that the farmer has more or less rounded the corner, and that he is well off now because the war is on. As a matter of fact, going over the farm income for 1942, though it has materially improved, I find that the total gross cash income for the average farm in Canada last year was 51,474.09. For Saskatchewan the gross cash income per average farm was $1,36121. That is the gross income. Out of that must be paid the threshing bill, hired help, taxes, insurance, interest on the debt, and farm operating expenses. Often these farms employ two or three persons; that is, the husband and one or more members of his family, all of whom have to get their income and sustenance, as well as their operating expenses, from the figures I have just mentioned.
The argument that has been advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) whenever we talk about better prices for farm products is that we are going to puncture the price ceiling. On March 22 he quoted a responsible minister in the New Zealand government, to show that in that country also they were extremely unwilling to alter their price structure. He quoted Mr. Sullivan as saying:
Thus, if stabilization brings about the fixing of wages or farm prices at their present levels, some sections of the community may feel that they are being made to contribute more towards stabilization than others. It may be only rough justice but it will be far preferable to the complete injustice which inflation run amuck would bring about.
I agree with that. But what the Minister of Finance does not tell the house is that in New Zealand a labour government which was elected in 1935 set about in 1936 to bring about a parity between farm prices and the prices of things the farmer must purchase. He did not say that they had been able to establish that parity price in pre-war years, and maintain it. The result was that when they did fix their price ceiling it was fixed on a more or less equitable basis as between agriculture and industry.
But that was not so in Canada. In this country the Minister of Finance took the arbitrary period from September 15 to October 11, 1941. He picked those dates out and said that they would be the base. All hon. members know what the situation was at that time. In 1941 the index commodity figure for field products was 56-5, for animal products 95-8 and for the average 89-9, and the figure for the cost of living was about 114. The last

figure for 1942, the latest we have-and I take it from the Economic Annalist, issued by the Department of Agriculture-indicates that even in 1942, although the situation was somewhat improved, the disparity was still marked. Field products were 66'4, animal products 107-4, the average 81-8 and living costs 118-4.
So that it is not comparable to say that New Zealand is maintaining its price ceiling, and that therefore our price ceiling is fair and that any interference with it is going to destroy our war-time economy. If the Minister of Finance is prepared to make the necessary adjustments to bring a depressed industry like agriculture up to the level of others, and then fix a ceiling, he will have no more hearty supporters than those of us in this group.
Someone quoted yesterday the Searle grain index which points out that on 147 items which farmers buy the figure is 153-7, the year 1913-14 equalling 100. The paragraph continues:
This means that these same things cost farmers of the west at the present time 53-7 per cent more than did similar items of the same quality in 1913-14. The price of wheat is now 19-9 per cent higher than it was in 1913-14. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is now, therefore, only 78 per cent of what it was in 1913-14.
We have heard discussions about parity prices. May I point out that so far as this group is concerned our discussions of the subject did not begin within the last year or two. We have been advocates of parity prices for farm products much longer than that. Our manifesto at Regina in 1933 said:
4. The restoration and maintenance of an equitable relationship between the prices of agricultural products and those of other commodities and services.
And our 1936 convention in Toronto passed this resolution:
The C.C.F. believes that similar legislation should be enacted immediately in Canada to provide for adequate returns and a proper standard of living for the Canadian farmer through a guarantee of minimum prices based upon the general level and price standards of other commodities.
When the Minister of Finance takes the stand that any argument about farm prices is an attempt to destroy the price ceiling structure he has set up, he overlooks the fact that already certain important commodities the farmer is compelled to buy have been allowed to break through the price ceiling structure.
Last fall, just about the time the farmer was going to buy lumber to build his granaries, lumber was allowed to increase to the extent of $12 per thousand. Repairs for farm implements have been allowed to go up. The price of newsprint has been allowed to go up $4 a

Western Grain Crop
ton. I am not complaining about these increases; they may have been necessary adjustments. But I am pointing out that some of the things the farmer has to buy have been allowed to puncture the price ceiling. It seems to me the time has come for a general revision of the price structure, so as to bring farm prices into line with those of other commodities.
The third point I would bring to the attention of the house with reference to the government's policy is that I believe it should accept some responsibility for assisting the farmer to carry his crop until it can be delivered. At the present time the entire responsibility of carrying the crop until the government is in a position to dispose of it is loaded entirely upon the farmer. He must finance threshing operations. He must meet immediate current costs. He must find material to build granaries and store wheat. He must look after his family, and at the same time pay interest on his debt. All this he must do without having received any of the cash income he expects from his crop.
In my own constituency last fall, in district after district farmers told me they were selling some of their stock in order to be able to pay threshers. Particularly was this so in the area where cars were scarce. There was a quota of five bushels per acre, and many of them had not been able to get space even for that five bushels. They had to sell pigs or cattle to get enough money to meet their immediate obligations.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did they have to sell stock before it was ready?

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, in some cases they were compelled to sell before they were ready, and in other cases they had to sell stock they did not wish to dispose of, or the disposal of which hurt their herds.
It is not the fault of the farmer that he could not deliver his wheat and coarse grains; neither is it the fault of the government. But the government has a responsibility in the matter. It has said, "You can deliver only a certain quantity. You can deliver it only as we have space and shipping facilities for it." Therefore it seems to me that some assistance will have to be given the farmer to help him through that period.
We suggested last year and the year before, and we are suggesting now, that an advance should be given on the deliverable portion of the farmers' wheat and coarse grains. It would not be a difficult matter to put it in the granaries, then to seal the granaries and give the farmer an advance of seventy cents on his wheat, basis Fort William. Give him an advance on his oats and barley until such time as it is possible for him to ship.
I certainly say the farmer is entitled to storage. As a matter of fact there is no better place for the storage of wheat than on the farms. That is the cheapest place it can be stored, and the farmer should be encouraged to store on his farm when he has enough room. He should be encouraged even to put up granaries, and the storage should be paid, as was done last year. One of the worst crimes one can imagine is to have wheat poured out on the ground, as I saw it in many places last fall, and covered over with sheaves or enclosed by snow fences to keep the cattle out, in the hope that it would survive the winter. When you consider that, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw very well pointed out the other day, that we may actually be faced with a shortage of grain on this continent, that in addition we may be called upon to feed the liberated peoples of the world, that the Minister of Agriculture has a tremendous programme for the production of beef, bacon, butter and cheese which in turn are dependent upon coarse grains, and that we have no guarantee that we are going to have good crops year after year, that one crop failure that would use up our surplus of coarse grains would mean a curtailment of the minister's live stock and bacon programme-

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister said last year that we had only one month's supply ahead.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not this year.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but if we had no coarse grains in 1943 the outlook for raising large numbers of stock in 1944 would not be very rosy. It would be a crime in my opinion if any wheat or coarse grain is allowed to rot on the prairies simply because the farmer cannot finance his crop until he is in a position to sell it.
I want to make another suggestion to the government in considering its wheat policy. The farmer's crop ought to be free from seizure by creditors. At present there is a great deal of bewilderment as to what the exact situation is. First of all, the municipality says to the farmer: You cannot get a permit to deliver your wheat until you have paid your taxes. That is right and proper. But some municipalities went further and said: You cannot get a permit until you have paid part of the seed grain advances of 1937 and 1938. That is a different story. To start to collect seed grain advances at a time when the farmer can deliver only five or six bushels and has all his obligations to meet was in my opinion a criminal act. But some of the municipalities did that.
Western Grain Crop

Then when the farmer gets a permit and begins to deliver the creditor steps in and says: We have a right to one-third of whatever is left. The quota may be ten bushels. The first four bushels may have gone for taxes and to meet other immediate obligations. Of the remaining six bushels the creditor claims two, leaving the farmer only four bushels with which to meet his threshing obligations and other expenses, rvhich cannot possibly be met out of four bushels.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Taxes were not taken out of the first quota.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Out of the first four bushels.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, not necessarily.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

I will say
this to the minister: I know very few municipalities that made provision for it. A great majority of them needed the money, particularly in the former dried-out areas, and they refused to give the farmer a permit until his taxes were paid. I do not blame them for that. All I am saying is that for a farmer to have to give the creditor one-third of the five or six bushels remaining, leaves him insufficient to meet his immediate obligations and carry on his operations. I suggest that the government take this matter in hand. It should not be left to the municipalities. After the taxes are paid the first ten bushels should be left to the farmer to meet his threshing bills and other obligations.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The municipalities are the ones who decide in regard to taxes.

speechtext: I was on the question of taxes five minutes ago. The hon. member should speed up his mental processes a little. I am talking now about creditors who have an agreement of sale or a mortgage which calls for one-third of the crop going to the creditor.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in mentioning that you said that the taxes took the first four bushels.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I had finished with that point. What I am saying now is that the federal government which took the responsibility of imposing this quota has the power, if it wants to use it, to say how the farmer shall dispose of that part of his crop which he is allowed to deliver.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The wheat board did that. They took care of the first quota.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Exactly, and after that what?

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where the municipality took care of the taxes the whole thing was taken care of in the first quota.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am referring to what happens from there on. The mortgage company steps in and claims one-third of the five or six bushels which the farmer has left, and that does not leave the farmer enough to meet his threshing bills and look after his family and carry on his farming operations. I am asking that the first ten bushels shall be free from seizure by the mortgage or loan company. The first charge will be the farmer's taxes, and I am asking that the remainder of the grain shall be the farmer's to pay his threshing bills and living allowance, and that the mortgage and loan companies shall wait until the quota goes over ten bushels.
I am also asking the government to see that steps are taken to deal with that part of the stored crop which belongs to the creditor. The farmer is required to store one-third of his crop, which is not the farmer's grain; it belongs to the creditor. The farmer has to store in his granary something which does not belong to him and although he is storing the creditor's crop the interest on his debt, for which the crop is payment, continues to grow. I do not think the creditor should have it both ways. Either the creditor should foe compelled to accept delivery or he should pay for storage. The interest on

Western Grain Crop
the farmer's debt ought to be stopped the moment the farmer puts the grain in the granary as payment for the creditor.
I want to suggest one thing more before I sit down. The question of debt legislation enters into the picture because the debt situation has been further aggravated by this grain marketing policy and by the delivery quotas which of necessity have been imposed because of the war. But there has been uncalled for delay. The decision of the supreme court was handed down last July. Since that date two debt conferences have been held in western Canada. Both have made recommendations and suggestions to the government. The provincial governments of the three prairie provinces have also made representations. Yesterday when the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) what action was being taken he was told that the Minister of Finance was greatly burdened. There is no one in this house who does not know that the Minister of Finance is greatly burdened and carries great responsibility. But the farmers are also greatly burdened; are the farmers supposed to wait until the Minister of Finance is less heavily burdened? Is there not someone in the government, some official, who could give consideration to this matter? We have waited month after month and no action has been taken. Some farmers have been, taken into court. Others are being harried and harassed. Others have signed quit claim deeds. An atmosphere of insecurity pervades all western agriculture. Up until now this government has done absolutely nothing about it except give the matter consideration. That will not do.
I ask this government to do two things: first, take the necessary steps-and it has power to take them-to stop all proceedings in the courts against farm debtors until such time as the necessary legislation can be passed in the house; and, second, to bring down in the house legislation under -which the machinery will be set up for adjustment of these debts at the very earliest opportunity.
These are the suggestions we make. 1. We ask the government that they close the Winnipeg grain exchange. 2. We ask that they accept delivery of all wheat and all coarse grains through the wheat board. 3. We ask them to assist the farmer in the carrying and financing of his crop. 4. We ask them to see that the first ten bushels per acre of the farmer's crop is free from seizure by creditors. 5. We ask them to take immediate steps to introduce debt legislation which will protect the farmer and give him security on his farm.
We have waited long enough for a statement. of policy from the government. I do not think we should be asked to wait any longer. This government's policy has been like a child's jigsaw puzzle; we get a little piece one day and a little piece another day. Every once in a while a minister pops up with another part, and we try to fit it in. Nobody is sure what the picture will be like when it is finished; nobody has any clear idea where the government intends to go. Bit by bit these pieces of the jigsaw puzzle come in. We want a statement of policy. We want to know what the government is going to do and how it proposes to do it. We have had enough of muddling. We have witnessed in the last two years the government blundering like an inebriated elephant on an acre of fly paper. The time has come when the government should place its policy before the Canadian people. If it does not, the tendency for men to leave the farms will continue, the tendency for people to throw up their tasks and go into other forms of enterprise will be accelerated, and this country may well find itself faced with a food shortage in the years which lie ahead.
I suggest to the government that the time has come for action, not for stalling, not for mere consideration. They must take steps now or face a complete break-down in agriculture, with all its consequences to the welfare of the Canadian people and our allies who look to us for their food supply.

I wish however to continue the remarks I was making at that time. I had been speaking of asking this house and this parliament for a sum of money for the purpose of developing agricultural research in Canada; and I had covered the uses which might be made of wheat, and of linseed oil from flax, and of sunflower seed oil from sunflower seed. I had intended to discuss the uses which might be made of the meals left after the oils are extracted from sunflower seed and flaxseed. These meals are very similar, though the one of sunflower contains a much higher percentage of protein than the flaxseed meal.
Some of the things which can be made from these products to-day are being made in the United States from the soybean. I believe that the use of these meals in Canada is an unexplored avenue in agriculture in this country, where by-products may be derived which can be used to great advantage.
For instance, strange though it may seem, these articles can be derived from the high protein meals I have mentioned: milk, butter, cheese, breakfast foods, diabetic foods, infant foods, bouillon cubes, soups, confections, coffee substitutes; Vitone, Ovaltine; a substance similar to the white of egg used in the confectionery business; protein sizings and protein plastic glues; oilless water paints, leather dressings, textile finishes, cosmetics, textile fibres of the rayon, wool or nylon type. Similar meals in the United States are being used to-day to produce plastics going into the manufacture of radios, refrigerators, and many parts of automobiles such as steering wheels, horn buttons, electrical parts, instrument panels, safety glass, plastic coatings for bodies; in fact, about fifty different parts of an automobile to-day aTe made out of this type of meal.
Plastic containers for food, to be used in place of glass sealers or to can foods, can be manufactured from the plastics made from these meals. As a matter of fact since I spoke in the house I have received a letter from the editor of one of our farm papers enclosing an article which stated that the

Macmillan Petroleum Company of California were using these plastic containers made from farm products in the distribution of their lubricating oils, thereby saving something like ten million pounds of metal per year.
Building materials can be made from the stocks and hulls of these two oil bearing plants. These materials have fine insulating qualities and are fireproof and waterproof. They can be moulded to shape in order to permit buildings being constructed without the use of iron or steel. Not only are these things possible; they are actually in use today in some parts of the world.
A great portion of the population of Italy and Germany are to-day clothed in wool made from casein, which is manufactured from milk. Milk casein makes a non-shrinkable wool which is easily dyed, is moth-proof and is difficult for even an expert to distinguish from sheep's wool. From milk casein can be made paints of all colours and fine glues which are impervious to moisture and which can be used in the lamination of wood for the purpose of constructing aeroplanes and aeroplane propellers. Milk casein combined with formaldehyde and heat produces a stonelike substance called galalith, which is used to-day under many names in the manufacture of fountain pens, bathroom fixtures, lamp shades, powder boxes, combs, cutlery handles, synthetic ivory and imitation amber and jade.
These are some of the things which can be made out of the farm products produced in this country. I hope the government will see fit to appropriate the sum I mentioned when speaking before, in order to carry on continuous research to discover new uses for our farm products and thereby create a more balanced economy in this country and give the farmer a better chance to live.

but I would remind them that two years ago, I think it was, I told one hon. member who interrupted me when we were dealing with coarse grains, that western Canada would produce more hogs than eastern Canada, and now the west produces a little more than twice as many hogs as the east.
I am getting a little tired of hearing hon. members from my province rise in this house and try to make out that the farmers of the west are all in terrible shape, that they cannot carry on, and that they must always lean on the government. I am a farmer, and I know the farmers pretty well. They have been asked to do a job in this war and they are doing it, especially the western farmers. For many years we as western farmers were chided in this house because we would not produce live stock. It was intimated that our people were lazy, that they liked to go to California in the winter, that they did not want to do anything except put in a crop and take it off, and have a holiday the rest of the time. Some people in this part of the country still seem to think that. I wonder if they think those hogs grow on trees out there. The western farmer is one of the most progressive men in this country, and when I say that I do not mean Progressive Conservative. You show him a job to do during the war and he will do it. You show him a way to make money to enable him to carry on without help, and he will do that too. During this war we have shown him that it is good business to produce live stock and dairy products. The minister tells me I am wrong in my figures as to hog production, but I have been looking at his own reports that come out every week, and from January 1, 1943, the order has been as I have given it, except that two weeks ago, when there was a tremendous storm out west, Ontario got ahead of Manitoba in marketings. That was for only one week, however, and in what I have said so far I am referring to the twelve.weeks period.
My hon. friend also spoke of the handling of coarse grains by the wheat board. Well, I think it was a little over a year ago that several meetings were held in Saskatchewan by the wheat pool at which the policy of the government in regard to wheat was criticized. I was at one of those meetings, which was also attended by the chairman or president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. He spoke from the platform, and I also spoke. I asked the chairman of the wheat p.ool if these were not the reasons that the pool was formed in the first place: First, for the orderly marketing of wheat; second, to sell through a central selling agency; third, to pay an advance price to the farmer and give a participation certificate;
fourth, to sell the farmer's wheat and to return to the farmer the best price that could be obtained in the world, less the actual cost of handling. The chairman of the wheat pool admitted on that platform that this was correct. He also admitted that, perhaps through no fault of their own, they had failed to carry out that policy. What ha3 been the policy of this government in regard to wheat? First, the orderly marketing of wheat; second, selling through a central selling agency; third, giving an advance price to the farmer with a participation certificate; and fourth, selling the wheat in the world market at the best price obtainable and turning over to the farmer everything above the actual cost of handling. That has been the actual policy of this government. That is what the pool was formed to do. If last fall the pools had wanted to be true cooperatives and pool coarse grains, there was never in the world a better opportunity to do so. A floor was put under barley and oats, below which prices could not go. The pools could have made that floor price the advance to the farmer. They could have pooled the grain for the farmer, had they wanted to carry on as pools, and sold it at higher prices, as it is being sold to-day, turning the money back to the farmer. But they did not do so; they dealt just as any other grain company did. They handled oats and barley for the farmer in the same way that any other elevator company would handle them.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), who, as I said before, is a good farmer, who knows a great deal about farming, and who had a right and indeed an obligation to get up in this house and discuss these matters. things have been forgotten by my hon. friend, because they are facts which would not show us up in a bad light.
The government of this country from the start of the war has worked out a sound agricultural policy. The farmer has been getting into a better position all the time. I have said previously in the house that we would need all the wheat and farm products that could be produced. I have said also that the only way to raise those prices is for the governments of the United States and Canada to get together and arrange between them to assume their respective responsibilities for the handling of the production of food for the allies. They must arrange for the shipment of that food. When that is done we may have a price structure as between Canada and the United States which does not show the disparity that exists to-day. But let me remind hon. members that while we are down on grain and live stock prices as compared with the United States, the man in the United States who is getting a higher price for his live stock, his butter or his eggs is paying a much higher price for his feed grain. We hear the argument that the Canadian farmer is not being paid enough for his field crops, yet he is not in a disadvantageous position compared with the live stock producer in the United States, simply because that producer pays so much more for the raw products which go into his finished article. The result is that he is not making a bit more money to-day than is the farmer in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not think I would have an opportunity to speak before six o'clock. However, there are some matters raised in the debate to which I should like to make reply.
The debate has covered a wide range of subjects. It has gone far beyond the marketing of wheat, which is the direct concern of my department. The -hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. Wright) has complained that the annual report of the Canadian wheat board for 1942-43 has not yet been referred to the committee on agriculture to which, I said, earlier this session, I should be very glad to have it sent. At as early a date as possible it is my intention to ask that the report be referred to the committee in question. As a matter of fact I should be quite prepared to do so now, were it not for the fact that members of the wheat board at this moment are, and have been for some time past, engaged in the serious consideration of vital problems affecting agriculture in Canada. The report to which reference has been made covers operations to the end of July, 1942.
The board has been here to consider various subjects discussed in the house yesterday and to-day. During the two weeks they have been here, interruptions have been caused in part by the discussion of problems facing various ministers of the government who are members of the wheat subcommittee of the cabinet. I am told it would be at the risk of having these problems suffer if members of the wheat board were now called before the committee on agriculture for the discussion of a report which, at the moment, is not of vital importance. I am not just sure how long it may take to straighten out the matters which require the immediate attention of members of the board, but it may be well on in April, possibly not until after recess, that I might feel I could properly ask them to appear before the committee on agriculture.
In this debate much has been said about coarse grains and the advance in price elsewhere beyond the ceiling. This problem has been giving the government much concern. Our anxiety is that the whole increase in price be returned to the producer, with the middle man receiving his ordinary normal profit. I am advised by the wheat board that in our anxiety in that direction they have the full sympathy and cooperation of the dealers in Winnipeg and of the grain exchange organization. The dealers do not want a profit beyond that to which they are properly entitled. As a matter of fact they call such a profit an unwelcome one because they are aware that it would react seriously against them.
A great deal of the oats which have been going to the United States and on which it has been stated that excessive profits are being made were contracted for before coarse grains reached the ceiling in Canada. A very large proportion of the coarse grains which have been shipped to the United States have been shipped merely in completion of purchases and contracts made when this situation of increasing prices did not exist. To avoid any of this profit going to anybody but the original producer the wheat board have handled the problem up to date by a restricted granting of permits. Quite recently the situation developed to a point where it was decided that other steps would have to be taken to control the spread in coarse grain prices. A new policy has been discussed and a submission prepared for council. I may say frankly that I had hoped to submit to council yesterday that submission from the wheat committee of the cabinet and from the wheat board. However, other matters of
16S4
Western Grain Crop

vital concern to agriculture in western Canada occupied council up to almost three o'clock, and to-day exactly the same situation prevailed but for another reason. I hope that I shall be able to get this recommendation for handling the coarse grain situation before the cabinet shortly and get its approval so that I can present it to the house almost immediately.
The hon. member for Melfort referred yesterday to some returns that he had been anxious to get. I understood they were in connection with grain matters, and I interrupted to say that the returns had been tabled that day.

Some of those participating in this debate have spoken as if the advance in wheat prices has not been a good thing for the farmers. This advance in the price of wheat is of direct benefit to the producer of wheat in Canada. If he has not yet delivered his fourteen-bushel quota, he can sell within the quota at the price prevailing on the Winnipeg exchange.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he can get cars.

speechtext: It is not a matter of getting cars, but one of being able to deliver within his .quota to the elevator. If his- elevator happens to be filled at the moment he is in exactly the same position as any other farmer who for one reason or another is not able to take advantage of the price of wheat on that particular day.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are the line elevator companies buying street wheat on the basis of the Winnipeg exchange cash prices to-day?

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. DOUGLAS (WEYBTJRN) ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unfortunately I am not able to answer offhand some of these technical questions. I have 
informed myself by consulting with my advisers, and I am advised that the farmer can sell at the advanced price on the Winnipeg exchange if he is able to deliver within his quota. I do not think there is any question in this house that the quota system has proved an advantageous method of handling wheat and has been accepted as satisfactory by the producers of the west. Even if the farmer has delivered his full quota, he stands to benefit by the returns from sales being made by the wheat board at the advancing prices on the Winnipeg grain exchange, which increased prices will be reflected in the participation certifications that the farmers hold.
I should like to say a word or two in connection with the direct benefit which the Winnipeg grain exchange has been in this situation. If it had not been for the buying on the Winnipeg exchange and for its operations, the only way in which the farmer could have reaped the benefit of an increased price over ninety cents was by the government arbitrarily raising the price of wheat and the initial payment to the western farmer. I think all hon. members will agree that such a policy would have met with resistance in certain parts of this country. The price prevailing on the exchange has afforded to the government an index of the market value of wheat, although we have a tremendous surplus of wheat which we are unable to sell.
The hon. member for Melfort criticized the government for making it impossible to ship wheat to the United States to take advantage of the higher prices there. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has dealt with that subject, but I will add a word or two.
What are the facts? The United States has placed an embargo quota against all higher grades of wheat from other countries, including Canada. The embargo applies to all over and above 800,000 bushels, and this quota, as has been pointed out, has already been filled.
It has been asserted more than once in this chamber that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture severely criticized the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with his method of announcing Canadian wheat and grain policy for the coming year. Very shortly afterwards, however, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture met by appointment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and certain members of the government; and in its representation to the cabinet it used these words:
Our organization recently expressed its regret that some features of government agricultural policy for the coming crop year had been announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce before there was opportunity to lay before

Western Grain Crop
the government expressions of views which were being formulated at that time. From assurances, since received from the Minister of trade and Commerce, it is evident that the occurrence in question was not due to any intention to ignore w'hat our organization might have to put before the government. The fact that this delegation is here to-day is accepted as further assurance that the government will be prepared to give due and full consideration to the representations which we are submitting.
I have been asked as Minister of Trade and Commerce to submit to the house the recommendations from the advisory committee to the Canadian wheat board. Frankly, personally I should like very much indeed to submit these recommendations. The hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) has asked for submission to the house of these and other documents. The matter has been delayed more than I had intended because I am giving close thought to the possibility of submitting that report to the house. What causes me to hesitate is that at the present time I believe it would be a breach of faith on my part to submit this report, which can, I think, be considered as a confidential or a privileged one, without first at least consulting the advisory committee. I can conceive of these carefully selected men-men who have been selected from the various western wheat pools, agricultural organizations in western Canada, the trade, and other similar organizations-hesitating quite a bit about giving their best advice- and I know that any advice they give is their best-to the government if they knew that this government would, in turn, make that advice public. However, the matter is under consideration, and I hope to make a return to the hon. member for Weybum within a very short time.
In connection with payment of farm storage on wheat, I hope to see the time in Canada, and that shortly, when circumstances will be such that every farmer will be able to have a reserve supply of wheat in storage on his farm. I remember, in the early days in Ontario, in going to my uncle's farm, seeing him with a fanning mill cleaning a load of wheat to take to town in order to buy various necessities. It occurred to me that that operation was very much like a bank account; and I think it would be a good thing for the economy of the country if we could get back as far as possible to each farmer being able to carry a reserve of wheat on his farm.
The trouble about the problem at the moment is not theoretical but actual. Our advisers tell us of the troubles they are facing in operating the wheat policy as announced by the government. Transportation has deteriorated tremendously since that policy was announced. There is also the matter of storage. These two factors, taken together, have led the government to decide that, at least at the present time, it cannot pay storage in respect of farm stored grain, for the reason that there would be a natural tendency to hold back that grain on the farm. In order to carry out our policy of taking 280 million bushels of wheat this crop year, we had to urge the farmers to deliver their grain at the earliest possible time. In this connection, at present we should have from one thousand to twelve hundred railroad cars a day to enable us with safety to accept what we have undertaken to accept within this crop year. After doing everything possible to improve the situation, we have succeeded up to the present time in securing from the railroad companies and other sources something less than five hundred cars a day.

The hon. member for Melfort raised a question as to the rights of the landlord and tenant in the fourteen-bushel quota of wheat. I am not sure whether the hon. member has seen the consolidated regulations of the wheat board which were issued in November, but since they carefully and clearly set out this situation I think I should put them on the record. Section 15 reads:
15. The producer actually carrying on the farming operations shall have the prior right to possession of the permit.
(a)	Whenever a quota of the grain produced on any land becomes deliverable, any producer entitled to a definite share of the crop as landlord, vendor, mortgagee or otherwise, shall be entitled to have delivered in his name a share of such quota proportionate to such producer's said definite share of the crop, and shall have full right to make delivery as a producer, and for such purpose the permit holder shall make the permit book available; provided that the actual producer shall be entitled to deliver the first five bushels of wheat permitted to be delivered for each authorized acre shown in the permit book, but such priority for delivery of the first five bushels shall not diminish the total amount of wheat which any other producer is entitled to receive and deliver or have delivered from the land covered in the permit book; this proviso, however, shall not apply
where the actual producer is merely a tenant under lease from a landlord and is not a mortgagor or purchaser.
Provided further that nothing in this regulation shall in any way derogate from, or interfere with any provincial law or enactment.
(b)	The enforcement of this regulation shall be the direct concern and responsibility of the interested parties themselves and no legal obligation shall devolve on the board in respect thereto.
(c)	"Actual producer" shall mean a producer actually engaged in the production of wheat. "Authorized acreage" and "basic acreage" shall mean the acreage for wheat delivery purposes established by the Canadian wheat board for the farm lands described in the permit book pursuant to regulations Nos. 3 and 4 above.
The hon. member for Lake Centre, in dealing with the problem, touched on a matter that is of great importance to many wheat producers in western Canada. That is the problem of damp wheat. It is a tragic thing for a producer with damp wheat who possibly has delivered his fourteen bushels, all he is able to deliver under his quota, to be told that in no circumstances is it likely that anything further can be done for him. He is to a great extent in the same position as the producer of higher grades of wheat in proper condition who has delivered his quota and still finds himself with a surplus to dispose of. The matter has been taken care of as far as possible by the wheat board furnishing cars to elevator points where farmers have damp wheat for delivery within the quota.

speechtext:
I
quite agree, and I am sure we all agree with the remarks of the hon. member regarding this particular difficulty that is being encountered in connection with the western wheat crop. All I can say at the moment is that the problem is receiving (he earnest attention of the wheat board and ourselves, and under our responsibility to the wheat producers of western Canada everything possible will be done to handle the situation.
It was suggested by at least one hon. member opposite that the government deserve some criticism for not having a long-range wheat policy. Nothing would please us more than if we were able at this time to formulate a long-term wheat policy. But world conditions to-day make that impossible.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) spoke of a farmer going to him, being anxious to deliver over the quota in order to meet certain liabilities. I am sure every hon. member who has any connection with western Canada has run across many such cases. He spoke of fourteen bushels. Put in that way, fourteen bushels does not seem much, but fourteen bushels is a pretty good average crop in western Canada. In addition, fourteen bushels an acre may mean, even to a small wheat farmer, two or three or four thousand dollars, and may mean many more thousands to the larger wheat farmers. Out of the proceeds of the quota of fourteen bushels T think any farmer should be in a position to take care of the demands of reasonable creditors. I have been in western Canada for a long time; I have never actually farmed myself although I have owned producing farms, but I have been close to the farmer in his troubles. My experience has always been that any farmer who is a reasonably good moral
I Mr. ,T. A. MacKinnon.]
risk had very little difficulty in dealing with reputable creditors. Deliveries over the quota in cases of that kind would merely make more difficult our problem, as I have already mentioned, in accepting the fourteen-bushel quota as promised.
The question was raised, I relieve by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), of the advisability of advancing to holders of farm stored wheat money by way of loan, possibly along lines similar to what has been done in the United States. I believe my information is correct when I say that the situation in Canada as regards granaries is quite different from that in the United States. In peace time a granary system was built up in the United States, so that now the farmer has, either on his land or elsewhere, proper granaries which can be sealed when a loan is made. I do not believe that in the great majority of cases in western Canada farm granary storage is conducive to sealing in this way. Of course at the moment there is very little possibility of doing anything by way of assistance in connection with the erection of granaries on farms, having regard to the very great shortage of lumber, nails and so on.
Then there was some criticism because there had not been any announcement of changes in our wheat policy. That wheat policy was submitted to this parliament at the earliest possible opportunity, for I had in mind the criticism in former years in regard to delays in submitting the grain policy to parliament. After very careful consideration, that policy was submitted to this house during the first few days of the session, so that the farmers might know the programme and make their arrangements accordingly. Minor changes in this policy may be brought about by unforeseen circumstances, but I can, assure hon, members that in the main the policy as submitted at that time will be the policy for the coming year.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Moose Jaw in expressing regret that so much talk has come from certain quarters as to the condition of blue ruin and desolation said to exist in western Canada. Our west is a great country. There are localities in which there have been conditions of real hardship, where conditions even now are anything but good, but on the whole the west is in better shape to-day than perhaps it ever has been. I am grateful to hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker, for the very fair and constructive speeches that have been made on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few remarks on the question now before the house mainly because some statements have been made which might mislead farmers as to the programme for 1943. I quite agree with hon. members who hold the opinion that sometimes thoughts which are expressed by some hon. members may be relied upon by some farmers throughout the country to a greater extent than announcements which may be made by the department, so that I consider it wise to correct one or two of the statements made and to place the facts on the record together with those speeches, in order that they may be read at the same time.
The first statement to which I wish to direct attention was made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and appears at page 1648 of Hansard for March 29, as follows:
When the Minister of Agriculture spoke in Saskatoon on January 15 he announced certain plans in connection with the production of wheat, oats, barley and rye. There was to be a decrease in the production of all these grains, but an increase in the production of mixed grains.
I call attention to this last statement in particular:
There was to be a decrease in the production of all these grains, but an increase in the production of mixed grains. There was to be no increase in the production of flax, but there was to be an increase in the production of hay and clover and a pronounced increase in the production of alfalfa. According to the news report of the British United Press, the minister went on to say:
"Mr. Gardiner stated that the price inducement to meet these goals and acreage payments will be revealed to-day."
I do not know what report of the British United Press was read by the hon. member for Lake Centre, but I have in my hand a copy of the British United Press report which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of January 16 and also in a weekly newspaper, the Alameda Dispatch, of January 22. This is what I find:
Here are the percentages of change in acreage required in 1943 as compared with 1942.
Wheat: 14 per cent decrease.
Oats: 12 per cent increase.
Barley: 11 per cent increase.
Rye: 31 per cent decrease.
Mixed grains: 1 per cent increase.
Flaxseed: No increase.
Hay and clover: 8 per cent increase.
Alfalfa: 17 per cent increase.
It will be noted that in mixed grains, which my hon. friend says was the only item in which there was to be an increase, that increase was only one per cent. Oats and barley both show a much greater increase.
Mr. Gardiner stated that the price inducement to meet these goals and acreage payments will be revealed shortly.
That does not say to-day. That was the report as it appeared in two newspapers which I checked, and it is a proper report of what was said at Saskatoon.
I should like to direct attention to the fact that there has been published by the Department of Agriculture this year a pamphlet entitled, "Objectives for Canadian Agriculture in 1943." This pamphlet contains forty-four pages and deals with every product that has been discussed here yesterday and to-day, giving the exact acreages that we wish this year, with the exception of flax with which I will deal in a few moments. It gives a report of what is desired in connection with all meats, all dairy products and all other farm products that are required in Canada this year, and it gives all the details the farmer requires in order to have the proper information with regard to these products. The point I wish to make is that this pamphlet is or will be in the hands of all farm organizations. It is or will be in the hands of all county or municipal councils across Canada. It is in the hands of all provincial departments of agriculture and, I presume, in the hands of all agricultural representatives sent out by provincial departments, and by the federal department of agriculture. There is, therefore, no reason why either hon. members or farmers should not be fully informed in regard to agricultural policies.
While I have been in the house-and I must say I am not in a position to say whether it was said while I was out of the house, and I have not had an opportunity to read all the speeches

the statement has not been made in this debate which was made so often before, namely, that a policy was never announced. Emphasis has been placed upon the fact that one change was made in the policy announced on December 9 last.
