What I wish to announce to-day is that so far as that change is concerned we are going back to the original request made of farmers on December 9 with regard to flax. We are asking farmers this year to grow about a million acres more flax than they grew last year.
May I repeat that the only change made in this announced policy from December 9 down to the present time, either by myself or by any official in the country who has been dealing with the matter, has been the change with regard to flax acreage and the necessary adjustment in wheat acreage. That has been discussed at some length in the house. I need

only mention to hon. members, particularly those from western Canada, one of the difficulties we ran into last year in relation to feed grain in order to emphasize the necessity for avoiding the same condition this year in relation to flax. We thought last year we had an assured market for all the feed grains we could grow in western Canada in any year. Our experience of the past led us to believe that we could anticipate a condition of that kind. We had marketed about 50,000,000 bushels of coarse grain annually, or probably somewhat less than that. And when we were discussing the possibility of marketing 200,000,000 bushels no one anticipated that anything could happen in 1942 which would make it impossible to market all our surplus feed grain. Every hon. member knows what happened in 1942.

Western Grain Crop
Our hon. friends across the way are not prepared to admit that the government showed any wisdom even in that matter, when we asked for a greater increase in acreage of feed grains than had ever been heard of in this country. They like to give all the credit to the fact that we had good weather conditions. I admit again that good weather conditions were necessary. But good weather conditions last year brought forth the very problem which has been discussed for the last two days on the floor of this house, the fact that grain is lying in fields all over western Canada. Not only did we produce the 200,000,000 bushels of coarse grain which we knew we might have a market for, and which we still hope we shall have a market for, but we produced 300.000,000 bushels more than that. And it is those extra 300,000.000 bushels which are the problem of the western farmer to-dav -those extra 300,000,000 bushels, or half of that amount at least.
What I should like to suggest to hon. members is this: Would they have advised in January of this year our going out and insisting on farmers producing another million acres of flax at a time when we were informed that there might be difficulty found in marketing that flax, because crushing facilities might not be available? What would hon. members have been saying to me as Minister of Agriculture in the last few weeks the house has been in session, if that information had been made known at the time the house met and I had not said to farmers, "Go easy in the matter of flax until we are able to announce something further with regard to your crop of this year." I have no doubt the farmers heeded our warning in that connection. But at the same time we stated that if there were to be any change in policy with regard to the acreage of flax, or the amount of flax which could be disposed of this year, that announcement would be made in sufficient time to allow the farmers to seed their flax this year, and have it available.
We did not leave it at that. We continued our negotiations with the United States. We entered into negotiations with the British government; and those negotiations have now advanced to the point where I can say with some assurance that farmers will be safe this year to sow an extra million acres of flax. And if they do, we expect they will be able to dispose of it.
Having said that, I should like hon. members, when they have this table before them,
to look at the two items of wheat and flax. I would ask them to place the wheat item back where it was in December when we asked for an 18 per cent decrease in wheat acreage, and to raise the flax item from "no change" to an increase of one million acres. Then the table will be exactly as it was intended on December 9, 1942, with regard to all farm products.

Mr. Speaker, at six

I had commented that on this occasion hon. members were not stating that no policy had been announced but had been paying some attention to one change which had been made in the policy as announced on the 9th of December last compared1 with what had been stated with regard to flax in January, 1943, and had suggested that we are now announcing that we expect the farmer to go back to the acreage asked for on the 9th of December, or to increase the acreage in flax by 1,000,000 acres. But in this debate, beginning with the mover of the first amendment (Mr. Wright), quite a number of hon. members have suggested that the policy was announced on this occasion without first consulting the farm organizations of Canada. I wish at this time to supplement what has already been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) by reading the correspondence between the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Department of Agriculture as a result of the discussions which took place at Calgary.
On January 30, 1943, I received the following telegram from Calgary, Alberta, sent by Mr. H. H. Hannam, president of the farm federation :
Hon. Jas. Gardiner,
Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa, Ont.
We register our protest against the action of the government in ignoring the action established in recent years providing an oppor-

Western Grain Crop
tunity for consultation with representatives of organized agriculture before announcing major farm policy. On previous occasions the Prime Minister and members of the government have stated that they welcome the presentation of our views and also the opportunity which this meeting afforded of discussing the position of Canada's basic industry with recognized representatives of primary producers. To-day in the closing sessions of the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture we learn from the press that the government has announced its grain policy for 1943. This has been done without having given an opportunity to this national federation of farm organizations to present their views and recommendations on this vital question. We realize the importance of an early announcement of government policy but delegates attending this annual meeting deeply regret this action of the government. They regard this as an indication of the government's intention to completely disregard the viewpoint of organized farm producers of Canada. For the past two years directors and officers of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have met with the Prime Minister and members of the government immediately at the conclusion of the annual meeting of the federation. This has provided an opportunity for farm representatives to bring before the government the considered opinion of organized agriculture from coast to coast dealing with its problems. We believe that at no time in the country's history has the need been greater for the closest possible cooperation between government and people. This will be impossible to attain if government creates impression that it proposes to ignore reasonable representations of organized producers. If the 1943 food goals as recently announced by Canadian government are to be met some upward revision of the income from grain should be considered. The annual meeting of the federation completes its session January 30 and will seek an opportunity of meeting the Prime Minister and members of the government at an early date. We desire to present our recommendations affecting agriculture including grain policy for 1943.
H. H. Hannam.
After receiving that telegram, I wrote Mr. Hannam under date of Ottawa, February 1, 1943, as follows:
H. H. Hannam, Esq.,
President,
Canadian Federation of Agriculture,
Toronto, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Hannam:
I acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 30th January addressed to me from Calgary.
I regret there has been any misunderstanding with regard to the grain policy. I understood the representations made by your delegation as well as the provinces at the December conference were that the government's policy re prices and reduction bonus was to be put out at the earliest possible date. The government considered announcement should be made to the house, and therefore made it at the earliest possible sitting.
All the proposals contained in your Saturday's resolutions as announced in this morning's papers were before us from farm sources when consideration was given to the policy for this year. There are only three variations from
(Mr. Gardiner.]
your proposals. Flax remains at $2.25 instead of $2.50. Wheat remains at 90 cents to farmers with no provision as to what it is to be sold at. You are, therefore, free to make further representations. The payment for grass for wheat acreage reduction has been at the rate of $4 in two instalments until this year. We propose to make it $2' for every acre of wheat reduction -without any complications this year. This had been discussed with western farm organizations.
I am sure a meeting can be arranged at which the government will be free to consider your representations made as a result of your annual meeting.
Yours sincerely,
James G. Gardiner.
I received under date of February 5, 1943, the following letter from Mr. Hannam:
Hon. J. G. Gardiner,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Gardiner:
This will thank you for your letter of February 1st. I have had a wire from Mr. Haskins this morning explaining that you have arranged for our representatives to meet the cabinet on February 9th, when, besides presenting our proposals having to do with other branches of agriculture, we may also make our recommendations in regard to the grain policy.
I do recall now, when you mention it, that the representatives of the -western provinces attending the dominion provincial conference in December did press for an early decision on acreage bonuses in order that they might be in a better position to know what change could be effected in wheat and coarse grain acreage. It happened, however, we had no representatives of the prairie provinces from our federation attending the conference.
We are grateful to you for having arranged for the cabinet interview as we requested.
Yours sincerely,
H. H. Hannam, President.
I think, in fairness to all concerned, that these letters should appear upon the record in order that members will believe what I have told them on two or three previous occasions, namely, that every matter dealt with in the wheat policy announced to this house had already been considered in the conference in December last and that at that conference the federation were invited to send as many delegates as they desired. They did send a number of delegates, and those delegates were present. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will remember that on that occasion both of us were asked to announce policies with regard to wheat acreage and with regard to price, to announce them not when the house met, but on the 9th day of December. When we stated in reply that the matter had to be considered in council before we could make an announcement, we were both asked to make that announcement at the earliest

Western Grain Crop
date possible. There was not a delegate in that conference who objected to that action being taken. Accordingly we followed the direction which we had at that conference, and on the first day on which it was possible to make the announcement after this house was convened, that announcement was made to this house.
I wanted to place that on Hansard along with the criticisms which have been made, in order that hon. members and others who read Hansard from time to time may be fully acquainted with what did happen. I repeat that we considered at the time that farm organizations had been consulted and that we had been urged by farm organizations, in common with those who attended that gathering, to make the announcement at the earliest possible date.
I might say in addition that when I was listening to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) reading an editorial from the Country Guide, published in Winnipeg, I recalled that the editor of that paper, who must have written the editorial or seen it, was one of the newspaper representatives at that conference in December at which this whole matter was discussed, he having been invited either by the government or the Department of Agriculture to be present and get all the information first hand, so that no misrepresentations could be made by others outside after the conference had been held.
The next suggestion which has been made, and with which I wish to deal for a few moments, is to the effect that the government left the farmer without provision to take care of his costs in connection with this year's crop, and more particularly to take care of his costs in the early part of the next season.
I would call to the attention of hon. members at least one provision which was made, and made at the request of the farm organizations, which has not been emphasized during this discussion, namely, the provision whereby any farmer who grew wheat prior to 1943, and has it in storage on his farm, does not need to grow wheat this year in order to be able to deliver his quota. If he has an amount equal to fourteen bushels to the acre for sixty-five per cent of the wheat acreage which he had in crop in 1940, he is permitted to deliver that wheat as soon as he can get it into the elevators following the 1st of August next. That is an assistance-and I think every farmer will recognize it as such-to the farmer in financing his operations during this summer. He does not need to worry about what the crop condition will be this year and therefore fear the possibility of crop failure if he has this wheat, which he has not been able to dispose of this
year, lying on his land. He can market, in case there is a crop failure, the other fourteen bushels to the acre which he grew, on the average, in western Canada, over and above the fourteen bushels an acre which he may have marketed. That provision was made, let me say, at the suggestion of farm organizations, and I think it is looked upon by farmers as one of the most important provisions which have been made.
Another criticism which has been raised is that this government has had no policy in connection with the marketing of wheat, especially during the war period, and an appeal was made to the house, particularly in dealing with the amendment which is now before us, that some policy be announced. In order to make his point the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) went back to 1935 and beyond, and placed before the house what he considered to be evidence of lack of proper policy in 1935 and improper handling of the wheat crops of 1935 and the years following. In making his criticisms he called attention to the fact that in one year the farmers were not permitted to deliver their wheat to the wheat board unless the price dropped below ninety cents a bushel-

Two years-the advance which was provided for in those particular years being 87J cents; and wheat had to drop below ninety cents before the wheat board would set up the machinery to take delivery of it. In almost the next breath the same speaker this afternoon called attention to the fact that the advance on wheat is,now ninety cents, and that immediately wheat went above ninety cents it is delivered, not to the wheat board, but to the trade. That is not a new condition. It has been the condition ever since we have had either pools or wheat boards handling wheat in western Canada. When the price has been above the advance which is allowed, the tendency has been to deliver almost all the wheat to the trade; when the price has been below the advance, almost every bushel has been delivered to the board and, therefore, to the government. So that this is no exception.
Having had that experience prior to and during 1935, the government did say the next year that there was no sense in setting up machinery for handling wheat which would not be delivered to the board, and that, therefore, until the price dropped to ninety cents that machinery would not be set up. As a matter of fact the figures quoted this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) demonstrate that the price did not drop to
Western Grain Crop

ninety cents. Instead of dropping, it went up during those years, and in going up, resulted in the delivery of the wheat to the line companies or to the pools which were prepared to buy the wheat from the farmer and buy it outright.
Again this year we are experiencing the same thing. That is one weakness of the pooling system which has caused trouble ever since the system was first set up. It was one of the weaknesses which we tried to guard against in the wheat policy which was set up in Canada in 1939, and which has continued to be in principle the same wheat policy down to the present time.
The change which actually has taken place is a change in the advance. It started out at seventy cents; it is now at ninety cents, the highest advance, as a matter of fact, ever paid by any government in Canada on wheat delivered to a wheat board since, or immediately following, the last war. The advance upon wheat is now ninety cents.
When anyone says that no preparation is being made to help finance the farmer, I venture to say there are few countries where wheat is grown in which greater assistance has been given to the farmer, and none in which so small a percentage can be marketed. In spite of the fact that so much must be held, the government says, "We are prepared to give you an advance of ninety cents a bushel on your wheat and you still own your wheat, if you deliver it to the wheat board." And if any such thing happens as is happening now, and wheat runs above that price, as it has during the last few days, the farmer will get the advantage of that advance to the extent that his wheat has been delivered to the wheat board.
There is one other matter with which I wish to deal in the few moments still at my disposal. It is the matter which was raised a few moments before six o'clock by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), and again by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Both of them referred to the fact that considerable discussion had taken place in this house session after sesion about the condition of the western farmer. I am sure every hon. member will agree with me when I say that since I took a seat in this house seven years ago I have done as much as any other hon. member to secure assistance for western farmers when they have been in trouble. There are people in Canada who have been kind or unkind enough to say that I am the Santa Claus of western Canada. Be that as it may, I know that people cannot

continue to live in a country which is being talked down continuously by those who represent that particular area.
I remember when I was first a member of the Saskatchewan government in 1922 or 1923 being invited to Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto to speak on a question then being discussed widely in the eastern part of Canada. This question had arisen as a result of editorials which had been running in a Montreal paper under the title "Whispers of Death". At that time there was a certain group of members in this house-none of them is here to-day-who were talking along the same strain as those members who in recent years have been talking down western Canada. They were telling about the terrible conditions we had out west. Sometimes we have had rather terrible conditions, but they were continuously talking about that.
I should like to give the other side of the picture. When I first came to this house seven years ago I was told by members on all sides of the house-I am not talking of any one side, although I am referring more particularly to the then leader of the opposition -that we ought to stop trying to grow wheat in western Canada, that we ought to move many, people out of western Canada, that never again would we be able to produce as we had produced in the years gone by, because the top of our soil had blown off, and so on. I wish to answer that to-night by saying that never in the history of western Canada has it produced a tonnage of food in four years equal to the tonnage that has been produced in the last four years. I am leaving the matter of price out of consideration altogether. We have produced many, many more tons of food from the top six inches of the soil in western Canada during the last four years than have been produced in any preceding four years.	.
That is my answer to those who said that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was not worth while in western Canada. That is my answer to those who said that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was not a proper policy to apply in western Canada. That is my answer to those who said only two years ago that wheat acreage reduction was not a proper policy to apply in western Canada. All these policies have been applied persistently and consistently in spite of criticism, largely from the far comer on the opposite side of the house, some from directly across the house, and occasionally some from one or two members on this side. However, the great majority of members in this house have supported those policies.

Western Grain Crop
They have believed that it is worth while to spend money to teach people how to live in an area as new as the great agricultural area of western Canada. Having taught them how to live, to-day we are appealing to them to produce the feed with which to produce the food in all parts of Canada necessary to feed the people of Britain, to feed our army, to feed our allies; to provide the necessary meat and dairy products. In addition, we are appealing to them to produce live stock products on their own farms. The hon. member for Moose Jaw was able to correct me this afternoon when he said that week by week during 1943 Saskatchewan was second only to Ontario in the marketings of hogs. These were produced to feed the people of this country and of Great Britain.
I come back to the point with which I started. Western Canada has demonstrated to-day, not only to the rest of Canada, not only to the empire but to the world that it is still an area to be. occupied by a prosperous farming population. In spite of some of those who represent our people in parliament, it is necessary to have credit to develop any new country. Western Canada required that credit and western Canada was able to get that credit. It is true that sometimes we found it difficult to pay our debts, and it is true that we are still finding it difficult to pay our debts. I speak subject to correction, and I shall make a correction later on if I find my figures are not exact; but when the delegation was here recently asking for debt adjustment legislation for western Canada it was pointed out that in an area where 156,000 loans are carried, only upwards of 10,000 farmers had asked for debt adjustment. When we so conduct ourselves in this house; when we speak in this house in such a way as to leave the impression that in this new area the farmers are going to rack and ruin because they are not able to pay their debts, I would' point out that while that may be true of a certain percentage of them, taking them at their own valuation, it is not a sufficiently large percentage for us to come to the conclusion that credit should not prevail in western Canada.
I think that to-day the west is fulfilling its mission as the great agricultural area of Canada. It is providing food for Britain and for those areas in Canada which consume more than they produce. It is providing the feed to furnish food. In connection with the matter raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Weyburn, I hope that no provision will be made, either because the government is not able to do so or because it is a matter 72537-107
of choice, to ship more than 200.000,000 bushels of feed grain out of western Canada this year. We have had sufficient experience in that part of the country to know that as nearly as possible we must carry a complete year's supply of feed on our farms until another crop is harvested.
Let me indicate what that means this year. We are told that we may not get another year like last year. I doubt if we shall, because it is the only one like it we have ever had. But it has been our common experience in western Canada that we get two good years, particularly when the first year is so wet in the fall that one cannot harvest all his crop. That is the best sign that we will get a fairly good crop the next year. The complaints which we hear about persons not having been able to harvest their crops last year apply to about fifteen or twenty per cent of the farmers of western Canada. The others got their crop harvested. The very fact that it rained to an extent that prevented fifteen per cent from getting their crop harvested in the three or four weeks of harvesting weather is an. indication that our prospects are bright for another good crop.
Even with that I would say, keep this grain on the farm to an extent to ensure definitely that we can produce in Canada next year the increased quantity of food that we are asked by Great Britain and by the United States to produce. Then, when we are sure we can produce that, we may be asked for more next year, and should keep sufficient in the west to be utilized along with anything we grow even in the fifth year.
I say that because I know farmers in western Canada who have not sold a bushel of grain for ten years; they have fed it all. During the last two or three years they have had to buy feed to finish their stock. On the same farms this year they are growing enough grain to feed all the live stock they have, and they have more than they ever had before. They have grown enough grain on some farms to feed it for four years even if they did not grow any more grain.
That being the case, I say again that this is not a time to be talking western Canada down This is a time to be talking it up; this is a time to be taking advantage of the feed that we have, and the fact that we still have some labour and still have opportunities to produce. I believe that next session we shall be able to come back to this house and say that we have produced more meat and dairy products in western Canada in this fourth year of the war than we ever produced before.

He has posed as the Santa Claus of western Canada, or has stated that that term has been applied to him. I think he is drawing on his imagination to some extent. At any rate there are a great many chimneys out west that he has not come down yet.
He referred to the production in the last few years. I would recall to him and to this house that Providence had something to do with that production. The very fact that Providence sent us the moisture he spoke about, which he says is an indication that we shall have a good crop this year, is evidence that he has not been the only one responsible.
I might say also that no one tries to discredit the producer; far from it. I do not think there is an hon. member who tries to do that. As far as I am concerned I think my record stands as one who has tried at all times-and I have had the support of my colleagues-to put up the case for the producer and to get something worth while for him, because he is always willing to do his part.
Yesterday the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) interjected an amendment that caused a number of speeches to be made. To-day we had another amendment moved by the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas), which provoked further debate and enthusiasm, and I think both are worth while.
The minister in replying offered certain excuses which indicate that the government may possibly do something. But it is time for action,.and that is what we want. The hon. member for Weyburn covered the whole situation, going back to 1930-35. I recall that in 1935 we passed the Canadian Wheat Board Act. We had a good deal of difficulty in getting that act through the house in the form in which it went through, practically as it stands to-day. This proves that it was a good act. I regret that we did not have at that time the support from all those who sat on this side of the house that we should have had. I recall July 1 of that year when the committee that had the framing of that act in hand met in the evening in the railway committee room, and the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who was a member of that committee, moved the final motion that that act be not operative after August 13 of the following year. That was strong opposition, and that is what we had.

Following that, we had an inquiry, headed by Mr. Justice Turgeon, into the grain marketing business. I have here the report, which is very interesting, and in view of this motion I think it would be well to consider some of it. Further, there was evidence submitted that the grain exchange could serve no useful purpose in times of emergency. Have we not an emergency to-day, and if that statement applies, what useful purpose can the grain exchange serve? In this time of war I think the government should be in full control. The wheat board is there; they have all the facilities to handle all the grain marketing business which to-day they are controlling by a permit and quota system of delivery, and one might say they have full control. I think the United Kingdom has also some say in the matter, since that is where most of our wheat has to go. I believe there are agents of the United Kingdom in Canada to-day who dictate to the board to whom

they shall deliver export wheat, where it shall be transferred for shipment, and in what ships it will be carried. So that the open market has very little control over the marketing of our wheat. It appears to me that under present conditions the United Kingdom more or less controls the wheat board.
Something has been said about speculators and what has happened recently on the Winnipeg grain exchange, in regard to the price of wheat. We have had a statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) to the effect that they have issued permits for the export of wheat and certain coarse grains, and yesterday we learned the number of permits issued and the number of bushels that have been exported. This is further proof that this organization must be controlled, and it would seem that this government and the wheat board are issuing permits for that purpose. I think this afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce might have given us a little more information. He referred to the fact that the committee on agriculture will not meet to consider the report of the wheat board for some little time yet; and even when it does meet to consider the last report it will be of very little value, since that report goes only to the end of the 1942 crop year. The minister should have told us exactly where we stand in regard to the wheat that is carried to-day by the wheat board'; the number of options they hold; the amount of cash grain they hold and the position it is in; the amount of advances, and so on. We cannot deal intelligently with this question unless we have that information, and now it seems the minister is taking the stand that we shall be able to deal with the report only up to the end of the 1942 crop year, so that we shall not be able to get any very useful information for this session.
I do not intend to refer at any great length to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said. He seldom makes a statement to the house, though on many occasions I have tried' to get him to do so. We did have a statement from him to-day, in which he dealt with certain matters and referred to the problems which the wheat board has to meet. Of course it has problems, but he says that those problems arise at least in part from the recent advance in price. If the wheat board is in full control, it need not worry about advances in price. The export markets are the ultimate destination of our wheat, and the wheat board should control that wheat. The minister referred to coarse grains

I move the following subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross):
That all the words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor.
"The policy of the government with respect to the marketing of Canadian field crops is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken forthwith to provide for the marketing of coarse grains as well as of wheat, by the Canadian wheat board, within the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 and amendments thereto; and that action should be taken immediately to abolish trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange in order to prevent speculation and profiteering at the expense of the farmers.
I think that covers the situation. We have the Canadian Wheat Board Act, with the wheat board in control. They should take over not only wheat but also coarse grains, and the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 should have full force and operation.
We have heard to-night from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) with respect to the coarse grains situation. He has pointed out that there will be a considerable carryover. Then the government could apply its new policy, which we expect to hear from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). We have heard from the Minister of Agriculture tonight that something is coming. Let the government review this subamendment and put it into force, because by so doing they will cover the situation and be a real Santa Claus to the people of western Canada.
It is not necessary to speak at further length. I have discussed at considerable length some of the important phases of the whole question. To-day's discussion has been along similar lines. Of necessity it could not be otherwise. I hope the government will see fit to adopt the subamendment.

Yes, they had been

In order that there

speechtext:
That is, that there
might not be any demand for durum wheat next year, as there has been in the past. It is just temporary.
When the Minister of Agriculture was speaking this afternoon he criticized those who credited the prevailing weather conditions for the grain crops, and he suggested that either he or the government should be given some credit. When he spoke I was reminded of a story that is told in my part of the country. I live right next to the Saskatchewan boundary, and I am occasionally informed as to what takes place in that province. The story is told that in one of the drought years a school teacher in southern Saskatchewan, after seeing a little shower of rain come up, quizzed the children as to who was responsible for it. After much hesitancy one little child put up a hand and said, "Please teacher, the Lord is responsible for it." But another child became very indignant, and she said, "You young
C.C.F'er, you should know better than that; Jimmy Gardiner is responsible for the rain." I did not think the story was so original until I listened to the minister this evening.
I do wish to agree with what was said by the Minister of Agriculture about what has been accomplished under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in the prairie provinces. Working with the minister as a member of an advisory committee, before coming to Ottawa, I had some experience in the matter, and on several occasions I have taken advantage of the opportunity to set forth what has been accomplished under that act, and what still may be accomplished not only in the prairie provinces but throughout Canada. I think there is great possibility in the reconstruction period, provided of course that we win the war, as I hope and trust we will. That board, by spreading out, can accomplish a great deal for the people of Canada. The act was brought in by the Hon. Robert Weir in 1935, and I am glad to see that its operations have been continued by this government. I have no doubt it will continue to operate for some time in the future. It has made a tremendous difference to the lives of many people in the prairie provinces.
We have had many discussions in the house about the price ceiling and parity prices. I
do not wish to repeat the argument as to how
Western Grain Crop

they affect the agricultural producer, but I must say that in my opinion there is no class of people in Canada to-day who would benefit as much by inflation as would the farmers. There is no argument about it. Nevertheless I as a farmer am in favour of the anti-inflationary policy in order to safeguard the welfare' of the salaried people of this country, provided that parity under the price ceilings is granted to all classes throughout the dominion. I think they are justly entitled to that parity.
I remember a grain inquiry which was conducted by Mr. Justice Turgeon. It held sittings throughout Canada, and at its Winnipeg sitting I presented a brief on behalf of the Manitoba Union of Municipalities. The present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) was counsel for that commission throughout its sittings. In presenting his findings, Mr. Justice Turgeon declared that in his opinion the grain exchange would render no useful purpose during a war crisis. I just mention that now on account of the present situation, where we have in the inner councils of the government to-day the man who was counsel for that grain inquiry commission. I think the finding of Mr. Justice Turgeon should be borne in mind.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext: The Minister of National Defence probably wrote it.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
He probably had something to do with it.
In seconding the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), which I trust the government will accept, may I say that the vast majority of the farm producers in this country want the Canadian wheat board to handle their coarse grains. The initial price to be paid by the board on oats and barley should be the present maximum allowed under the ceilings, and participation certificates should be issued to the producer on the same basis followed in regard to wheat, so that if any profit is made over and above the initial price the producers will share in the returns.
I have cited the finding of Mr. Justice Turgeon that the Winnipeg grain exchange can render no useful service during this war crisis. May I add in conclusion, that the farmers represent one-third of the population of Canada, and a very great percentage of them are grain producers. I believe that the amendment represents their wishes, and I trust that the government and parliament will give it due and proper consideration.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, if I were living in the 
constituency of Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, I would undoubtedly vote for the present sitting member (Mr. Perley). I have no prejudices. If I were living in the electoral district of Melville, Saskatchewan, I would vote for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). But of course I am not a citizen of Saskatchewan. I am an easterner, and may I be permitted to-night to express the views of an easterner with regard1 to the wheat situation.
I have the highest regard for my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), but I have never understood why wheat was separated from other agricultural products and was placed under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, while all other agricultural products come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. Second, I do not understand why in the last twenty years no easterner has been appointed Minister of Agriculture in the federal government, and I say that without intending to cast any reflection upon any of those ministers. I remember that- in the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier the Minister of Agriculture in the federal government was doubly an easterner. He came not only from eastern Canada but from the eastern townships in eastern Canada. That was the late Hon. Sydney Fisher. And the first Minister of Trade and Commerce was that great Liberal fighter whose name is not forgotten by any true Liberal, especially in Ontario, Sir Richard Cartwright. I will go further and say that if I were a constituent of Moose Jaw I would undoubtedly be filled with enthusiasm by the eloquence of the present sitting member (Mr. Ross), and would vote for him with my two hands.
Wheat is the food par excellence. When I was a child I was told by my grandmother never to waste bread. I remember also that one of the greatest kings of England told his son never to indulge in wheat speculation because it was.unfair to the poor, and he reprimanded him for doing so.
Listening to the speeches, and1 they have been most interesting, which have been delivered by all those who have spoken on this question, and reading Hansard to become more familiar with the arguments made by each one of my hon. colleagues who have discussed the matter, I feel that one must come to this conclusion, that in the wheat business the great offender is neither the producer nor the consumer; it is the grain broker;

Western Grain Crop
it is the Winnipeg grain exchange. That is the conclusion of the argument that has been made.
I remember that during the last war our western producers were supreme in the British market. At that time they had no competitor in South America. I also remember very well an article that was published in a Toronto paper by the late Hon. Frank Oliver who had been Minister of the Interior in the Laurier government-he was a westerner too-to the effect that the west had killed the goose that laid the golden eggs. He meant by that, that westerners had themselves been responsible to a large extent for the loss of the British market for grain as a result of the exorbitant prices that were charged to British consumers. The authority is good; it is that of a man who knew the west better than perhaps, any one of his contemporaries. I remember that when Mr. Bennett was in pow'er, the then member for Rosetown-Biggar, Mr. Loucks, who had a seat somewhere near here, was laughing and jeering when I was saying that. But it is a fact that the British consumer was exploited by those who were selling wheat to him, and that is precisely the reason why such an amount of British capital has been invested in South America, particularly in the'Argentine republic, for the growing of wheat. Was it the western farmer or the western broker or the Montreal broker or the London brokers who were responsible for that exploitation of the British consumer? It is not for me to tell. The facts are there. But the fact remains that the British consumer has been exploited by the westerner, and this is the reason why new fields of wheat have been cultivated in South America.
We have heard a great deal about markets -markets which were not defined. .What is the market now for our wheat? The first market for Canadian wheat must be our own country. Very few hon. members have mentioned that Canada is our own market for wheat. The second is all friendly countries where Canadian exports are possible. Of course there is a limitation on account of the war. But wheat is not perishable when it is not exposed to moisture; it keeps for a long time. Hon. members must remember photographs which were published in several periodicals showing wheat which was preserved in good condition in King Tut's tomb. Wheat may keep for a long time; and if at the present time we have at our disposal the markets of friendly countries, why not keep a reserve of wheat for the bad days which will follow the war, when Canada will have an
opportunity to export wheat not only to friendly countries with which we can deal now, but also to friendly countries which are now occupied by the enemy, and even to enemy countries?
If my memory serves me aright, I cannot offend the patriotism of any of the Progressive Conservative party or group by saying that, because the very last provincial government of Canada to export wheat to Germany, on the eve of the war, was precisely the government of Manitoba which was then headed by the new chief of the Progressive Conservative party, and he did it under a barter arrangement, exchanging that wheat for some machinery. But that happened on the eve of war. Do you not think, sir, that, as soon as the war is over, the first policy of all governments will be to deal as much as they can with all countries of the world, whether they have been friends or enemies? Therefore, future trad* must be considered, and trade may do a great deal in the fixing of the price of wheat.
I cannot understand the various policies of various governments on wheat; they have been so contradictory that they make one seasick. Think of it! We had every sympathy for the westerner when he suffered from the drought. On the other hand, instead of the farmers of that area being moved to more fertile parts of the province or of the country, enormous sums were spent for irrigation and to restore the fertility of that dry soil. That was done, and after it was done to increase production, what was the next step? ^ Farmers were paid not to cultivate wheat. It is absurd. On the one hand, all the irrigation works to improve that area which suffered so badly from the drought; on the other hand, curtailment of the production of wheat. Each of these policies is in conflict with the other. It shows that if one plan was good, the other one was wrong. This is a thing which I cannot understand.
Another thing which I cannot understand is the picture which the Minister of Agriculture has made of the west without saying a word of the east. According to what he has said, the western provinces are the Garden of Eden of Canada. I do not deny it; it may be true. But we easterners have been told for such a long time that we must consider Canada as a whole as our country, that I find that the speech which was made this evening by the Minister of Agriculture is rather parochial. This is why I would have voted for him if I had been on the electoral list of Melville. According to him, we are doing everything in the west; we are feeding the world; it is the prairie provinces that do that.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Western Grain Crop

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
I do not deny that the
prairie provinces are doing their part, and I congratulate them upon that. But, as one comes east, Canada does not stop at the great lakes. Canada is a country that extends from coast to coast. If this speech had been made by a minister of agriculture from the east, the excuse would have been made that he was catering to the west. But it was made by a gentleman who comes from the west and- who is talking only for the farmers of the west. That is not fair treatment for the farmer who toils in the east.
We hear the old story of the feud between the east and the west. We hear the question: Who has done more for the economic life of this country? The westerner says, "We have been, enriching the east," and the easterner says, "We have been paying for the west." That is the whole story. Nobody cares, and the feud goes on and on and on; there is no end to it. We hear the same story every session. I have stated before that the western farmer has received privileged treatment from all governments since I have been a member of parliament. It was worse under the Bennett regime, but it was continued by Mr. Dunning as Minister of Finance. Hon. members will remember what happened. In the first place there was a guarantee. That guarantee then turned into a loan. Finally the guarantee which has a metamorphosis and emerged as a loan, ended up as a gift. To use a botanical expression, it was just like the dandelion which had changed three times.
Why was the same treatment not given to Ontario and Quebec? The reason w'as that these two provinces were too proud to say that they were insolvent. The western farmer went to his municipal council and said, "I need help; I am broke." The municipal council went to the province and said, "We need some help; we are broke." Then the provinces came to Ottawa like the burghers of Calais with ropes round their necks and said, e are all broke; we need something." Because the eastern provinces did not use the same method of trying to get subsidies, they got nothing. It was thought that they did not need it, that they were not insolvent. The open sesame for the exchequer was insolvency. As soon as that was pleaded, all doors were opened and the money flowed into the hands of the western producer. It may look strange, but that is a fact. I asked Charles Dunning about the payment of interest on the loans, and I asked him if any of the capital had been paid' in Saskatchewan. He said none had been paid and also very little interest. Apparently Saskatchewan was the worst
tMr. Pouliot.]
offender. Why, I do not know. That is the way in which the farmer of the west has been aided. He has been given every opportunity, opportunities which have been denied to the easterner.
How long does it take the easterner to get coarse grains from the west for feeding purposes especially for the raising of hogs? It takes a Jong time on account of traffic conditions on our railways. The situation is so bad that our farmers cannot get grain from the west. Then we talk about export trade. How can we export out of Canada when we have not sufficient means to transport this grain to the farmer consumer? There is no reason why the eastern farmer should not be given the same subsidies and the same help that is given to the western producer. We are three thousand miles closer to Great Britain. There aie harbours and ports on the St. Lawrence with every possible loading facility; yet they are not used. There should be an energetic policy drafted and acted upon at the earliest possible opportunity.
I referred to the feeding of hogs, but there are some human beings who need grain more than do hogs. There are many people in the large eastern cities and in other centres of the east who do not have enough to eat. Why does the Department of Agriculture not see to it that rolled oats are made from oats, and flour from wheat, and then send these products to the needy people in this country wherever they may be, whether in the east or in the west. That is a humane policy to adopt. There are many needy cases. During the Christmas season the greatest paper published on this continent, the New' York Times, gives details of many needy cases in the United States metropolis, and eloquent appeals are made for charity.
In my humble view reforms are needed in connection with this wheat question. In the first place the link between the producer and the consumer should be shorter. It should be easier for the consumer to get wheat and other grains produced by the western farmer. We give wheat to other friendly countries; there have been large shipments made to the United Kingdom as gifts. Why not serve our fellow citizens when we can do something for those outside this country? You do not know, sir, how painful it is t-o think that Canada at the present time is a forgotten country. It is a country where the man in the moon lives.
It is a country that is out of the planet where war is raging. Let us not forget that our first duty is to our fellow citizens, that we must think of them first. What was the first thing that that great Liberal, Franklin D. Roosevelt, did in the United States to improve the health

Western Grain Crop
of the American people? It was to feed them, to feed them well, to give them good food. That was his first step for national recovery. In this land of plenty there is no excuse for not following such a wise example, to see to it first that our fellow citizens shall eat flour from the west, eat rolled oats from the west. They should get it very easily. I do not wish to cause any embarrassment, but I could go further. Why do we not make better use of grain? Why is better use not made of grain for liquor, for instance for gin? Some hon. members perhaps find it amusing, but it is much deeper than that, for two reasons. In the first place in a previous session I had an opportunity to mention a certain concoction that is a compound, called compound gin, because it is not gin. The formula for gin is that it is a liquid made of the distillation of grain, redistilled with juniper berries and other aromatic herbs. When I was denouncing the way in which compound gin is concocted, western members did not think at the time that I was fighting their cause.

speechtext: Can western wheat be used to make gin?

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
No; they can make it of barley and rye, but it must be grain. The formula does not mention any special kind of grain. But to prevent the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) from being poisoned, I will tell him how compound gin is manufactured. After the sugar is extracted from the sugar cane, there is a certain amount of trash left. It is that trash, which formerly was swept away, that they are now redistilling to make a kind of alcohol that is something like industrial alcohol, which is then mixed with a kind of syrup like cariboo, and it was advertised as pure gin at the expense of the western farmer and at the expense also of public.health. I regret that that practice was not stopped and that the department concerned did not stop that false advertising of a compound as genuine gin. I could say much more about it, but I may have other opportunities. It is like a novel; there are some incidents that may have more of the picturesque than words can describe.
Now, sir, is it possible for the Canadian farmer of the east to have equal rights with the western farmer?

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext: No chance.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, " no chance." I should like to have him as minister of agriculture. I know him; I have been in his county speaking for him, and if I am invited I will go again. I have a great admiration for him. I wonder if it will be necessary to have 72537-108
an easterner as minister of agriculture in order to have fair play for the eastern farmer. I hope the present minister will in due course show that he is wise enough to understand the eastern problem as well as he has the western problem, and since we are giving away millions of dollars to other countries, why not give the eastern farmer as much as has been given in the past to the western farmer?

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
I propose to deal now with the relevancy of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). If any hon. member wishes to speak on that point, will he do so now?
The motion is that the house go into committee of supply, to which an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). A subamendment was moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross):
That all the words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"the policy of the government with respect to the marketing of Canadian field crops is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken forthwith to provide for the marketing of coarse grains as well as of wheat by the Canadian wheat board, within the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 and amendments thereto; and that action should be taken immediately to abolish trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange in order to prevent speculation and profiteering at the expense of the farmers."
The subamendment differs from the original amendment. In the original amendment all that is asked is that the house desires to record its opinion that the grain marketing policy of the government is detrimental to the public interest. In the subamendment what is asked is that steps should be taken forthwith by the government to provide for the marketing of coarse grains. That is a matter involving public expenditure as I indicated last night when dealing with the amendment made by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), and I therefore rule it out of order on the ground that the expenditure of public money could not be moved by a private member.
In his new book on Parliamentary Rules and Forms, published by our Clerk, Doctor Beauchesne, which I now have before me, the third edition, 1943, will be found on page 710 a decision given by Mr- George Black, then speaker of the house and now the hon. member for the Yukon. That decision stated:
A private member cannot move, on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for committee of supply, an amendment to the effect that the

Western Grain Crop

government should proceed without delay with a certain undertaking involving an expenditure of public money.
The subamendment is in almost the same words, or at least the conclusion would be the same. The words are, "that steps should be taken forthwith", whereas in the decision of Mr. Speaker Black the words were, "that the government should proceed without delay." In that instance there was some question in regard to the legality of a claim by the province of Quebec, which of course would involve a certain sum of money, and also a question in regard to the incorporation of the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company. A point of order was raised, and Mr. Speaker Black ruled it out of order. In his opinion the resolution if passed would be a direct order from the house to the government to do certain things which would involve an expenditure of public money. Therefore he held that such a resolution is not in order when moved by a private member.
Further in Beauchesne, third edition, paragraph 461:
On the 20th February, 1926, a member moved that the government be requested to "immediately" introduce legislation granting adequate retiring allowances to all citizens over sixty years of age. The Speaker ruled the amendment out of order on the ground that it involved the expenditure of public money. An appeal was taken from this decision but the house approved the Speaker by a vote of 158 to 2.
In my judgment, therefore, the subamendment involves the expenditure of public money on the part of the government and cannot be introduced by a private member. Therefore I rule it out of order.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
In regard to the ruling just given by Your Honour I should like to make this observation. I take it there is no objection to the moving of an amendment to in amendment on going into supply. That principle, I think, is well established and has been followed by this house on many occasions. The point just raised by Your Honour, however, I think might properly be given further review in this case. The amendment to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) is in these words:
The policy of the government in respect to the marketing of Canadian field crops is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken forthwith to provide for the marketing of coarse grains as well as of wheat by the Canadian wheat board, within the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 and amendments thereto; and that action should be taken immediately to abolish trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange in order to prevent speculation and profiteering at the expense of the farmers.
Mr. Speaker.]
With very great deference I would point out to Your Honour and to the house that with some regret, if I may say so, I find myself unable to agree with your ruling in this instance. While it may be said that we in this house long ago adopted the principle that a private member may not move an amendment such as this which involves the expenditure of public money, at the same time I would suggest that this amendment does not fall within that class. The Canadian Wheat Board Act, which is chapter 53 of the statutes of 1935, contains the following as section 14:
The governor in council may approve of the provisions of this act being made applicable to oats, barley, rye or flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if the board recommends that such approval be given, whereupon the provisions of this act shall mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
My point is that under that act the principle actually has been adopted and approved by the parliament of Canada, and that principle having been adopted and approved, then I suggest that Your Honour should not find that this amendment would mean the expenditure of additional public funds, which is the point dealt with by the rules. For that reason I find myself unable to agree with your decision, because in this amendment we are not departing from the rules to an extent which would actually mean the adoption of the principle of expending public money on the motion of a private member, since the principle at issue already has been approved in the act which is mentioned in the amendment itself. If the amendment had not included those words; if it had not specifically mentioned the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, then I think we might perhaps have been able to accept the ruling Your Honour has seen fit to deliver, but with great deference I suggest that in this instance the amendment to the amendment does not actually involve the expenditure of public money which has not already been approved by the parliament of Canada.
That being the case, I would respectfully appeal from Your Honour's ruling.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
I do not know whether or not the matter of the appeal is debatable at all, but after the ruling was given my hon. friend raised the point, and it seems to me that if he really means that there is to be a formal appeal, one might have an opportunity of saying just a word in regard to it.
My hon. friend has indicated that Your Honour's ruling is not valid, because, as he suggests, in the Canadian Wheat Board Act

Western Grain Crop
there is provision for the marketing of coarse grains by the board, provided it is so ordered by his excellency the governor general in council. That is exactly the point. His excellency the governor general in council, that is to say his excellency's advisers, may order the marketing of coarse grains by the wheat board and the expenditures which would be occasioned, but that does not involve the principle that a private member of this house, who is not one of his excellency's advisers, has a right to attempt to commit this house, without motion of his excellency's advisers, to such a course. It seems to me that my hon. friend has entirely missed the point, that it is the governor in council that has the power under that act.

speechtext: The principle has been adopted in the act.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext: The principle has been adopted of permitting his excellency's advisers to decide whether or not such an action should be taken.

speechtext:
I permitted the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) to make his remarks, though I had invited any hon. members who had any remarks to offer to make them before I gave my ruling. It is quite irregular to have a Speaker's ruling the subject of discussion after the ruling has been given. The only reason why I permitted it was to give the leader of the opposition an opportunity to show me how, in his opinion, my judgment or opinion was wrong. Naturally, had it been made clear that my decision was wrong, I should have been glad to be corrected.
Having listened to the leader of the opposition, I did notice that in the course of his remarks he referred to an amendment such as this-and I think these are his exact words- "which involves an expenditure," stating that it did not come within the purview of the principle I endeavoured to apply last night, and in the present instance. The provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, are subject to the judgment and control of the government operating the act. If there is an expenditure to be incurred under that act, it must necessarily be approved by the government. And if the government feels an expenditure is required, then, of course, according to the principle which is well established, and which has been recognized at all times, the government alone can deal with the question of public expenditure, and private members therefore cannot.
In the decision I quoted of Mr. Speaker Black the same ruling w'as established, and was recognized by the house, Nothing has been said to change my opinion as to the sound-72537- 108J
ness and validity of the ruling I have given. I therefore must rule accordingly.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
am glad of the opportunity which this debate affords me to make some further remarks on agriculture. As stated many times in this house, farming is essential to the prosecution of the war. It supplies the soldiers with food, clothes and lodging. It feeds the war industry workers and the civilian population. Will Canada, an outstanding wheat-producing country, let its government wreck agriculture by depriving it of its best workers? No member of this house can think of the agricultural overproduction which is now so urgently needed without thinking also of the thousands of farmers who are still in military training camps.
What happened last year at wheat harvest time in the prairie provinces? Wheat producers even had to enlist the help of students from the east in order to harvest their crop. Those young men, most of whom had no experience, have done their work with matchless devotion. But how many bushels of wheat have been lost through the labour shortage? In many areas of the west the wheat crop was snowed under before the producer could harvest it. That did not happen only in the case of the wheat crop in the prairie provinces. In British Columbia thousands of barrels of fruit could not be picked. That was also true in the Niagara peninsula and in countless other areas in the eastern provinces.
Should the government not be condemned for having thus failed in their duty to the producer, the consumer and the army?
At a time when we ration the food that is so essential to our hard-working fighters, at a time when Canadian soldiers cannot have the foodstuffs that are essential to their health and sustenance, we are witnessing the sorry spectacle of our wheat and fruit crops being spoiled. Is it to be wondered that sugar, butter and meat should everywhere be so scarce? That is the price paid for the carelessness of a government which has denied to farmers complete and definite exemption from military service. Such are the disastrous consequences of a short-sighted policy which persists in refusing to withdraw from military camps and send back to the land the thousands of farmers who are still in training. Of what use is the short six-week leave announced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), a leave granted without pay and without travelling allowances to some classes of men, and in such a small percentage that it borders
Western Grain Crop

on cynicism? Will the government never be able once for all to forgo half-measures and face the situation squarely? Opportunism and laissez faire have prevailed for too long under the present administration who, taking advantage of the secrecy of the cabinet, govern by orders in council, over the head of parliament. On March 12 last the cabinet passed an order in council to authorize sending overseas recruits called up for the defence of Canada and of Canada only. This house was not informed of this fact until ten days later. It is alleged that such action is for the defence of -democracy. And these so-called defenders of democracy trample underfoot responsible government and democracy itself. How many farmers are there among these young soldiers *who are sent to Jamaica and to Newfoundland? We shall never know. Secrecy will forever veil this great adventure that history itself will record among the unfulfilled promises.
Speaking in this house on March 23 last, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Poirier) alluded to the speech I made on March 9 in this house. I am grateful to the hon. member for all the kindness and all the interest he shows in connection with my statements. However, my hon. friend ought to know-as he probably does-that at the time I was speaking on the price of wheat flour, I had in mind the conditions in which not the wholesaler nor the federated cooperative, nor even the small retailer, but the consumer of my locality found himself and who, I repeat, pays almost $4 per 100 pounds for wheat flour, or exactly S3.75 and $3.90.
I would remind my hon. friend that in my constituency wheat sells at $1.70 per hundredweight. I know something about it as I have been keeping poultry' for a number of years. For laying mash the consumer pays $2.90 while Growena or chicken feed sells for as much as $3.10 and $3.15 per hundredweight. I will not accuse my hon. friend, as he accused me, -of deceiving Mr. Speaker and the house. But I do not mind saying that the hon. member misrepresented me and gave my' words a meaning which they have not or never had. Since my hon. friend takes offence because I stand up for the consumer and the farmer against the great millers and the bogus middlemen who have both been exploiting them for many years, I suggest in all good faith that he , himself provide better protection for the fishermen and the farmers of his constituency against the mobilization act. My' hon. friend will recall that, on February 19, 1942, when he voted against our amendment asking for the exemption of his constituents from military service, he accepted in principle the mobilization and conscription of his own people.

Incidentally, I may say that I hold the hon. member in high esteem and I feel sorry if his attitude has forced me to restate this question. I decline all responsibility for the matter. He shall answer for his attitude to his constituents. I decline all responsibility in the matter except I have only discharged a splendid duty to the farmers and fishermen of Bonaventure, Laval-Two Mountains and the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I am no flatterer and I take no part in the vast concert of praise being performed on fiddles big and little. I shall support worthy measures from any quarter and oppose any policy which I consider inimical to the country's interests. Honourable members who take part in this debate are fully justified in condemning the government's attitude toward the wheat producer. When a country spends or makes an outright gift of billions after its government has made bold to subsidize acreage reduction; when a nation rations the necessaries of life and then goes so far as to pay the producer for stopping production, when we think of the sordid bill of fare of the poor whose families are always larger than those of the rich; when we see the Canadian mother's inability to perform the miracle of providing her ten, twelve or fifteen children with the sugar, milk, butter and meat required for their normal growth and development, are we not justified in asking ourselves what sort of country we are living in, what sort of government we have, and if we are not threatened by famine, ruin and disaster?
