Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak again in this debate, but certain statements have been made which I feel it is my duty to correct in order to keep the record straight. One of the last offenders was the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot). He would give the house the impression that the west has received all the privileges, and the east the small end1 of the deal. I cannot agree with that, and for his information I would state that while the west has supplied most of the Ministers of Agriculture in past years since the hon. member has been in this house, the east has supplied the Ministers of Finance, and the Minister of Finance has generally made a very effective job of controlling the policies of the Minister of Agriculture. If the hon. member cares to investigate that statement, I think he will very easily be able to verify what I have said
Practically all the products that are marketed iby the eastern provinces are at or above parity prices if you take the 1926-29 average as a basis. Butter is four cents up;

Western Grain Crop
cheese is 6-1 cents up; eggs are 1-3 cents down; steers are 24 cents up, and hogs are 67 cents up. All of these products are marketed mainly by eastern Canada.
In the west we produce wheat and coarse grains below the cost of production and far below parity, and ye.t the government pays freight on our feed coming to eastern Canada. I will give the hon. member for Temiscouata some figures that he should have heard before this evening. Our wheat is down 544 cents below parity; oats is down 9 cents below parity; barley is down 11-2 cents below parity, and rye is down 384 cents below parity. These figures should be sufficient to indicate to the hon. member for Temiscouata that the east is getting its fair share and a little more. That is what is happening, in agriculture.
But the hon. member for Temiscouata will also realize that western Canada contributes to the loan and insurance companies located in central or eastern Canada. He will also know that war industries are located in eastern and central Canada. So that, on the whole, eastern Canada is pretty well taken care of.
I want to thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) for the announcement he made yesterday that soldiers' grain will be taken care of in the case of those farmers who have been drafted into the army or have volunteered for active service. I was very glad to hear the minister make that announcement. I consider it only right that this action should have been taken because these men are already making their contribution without having to worry about their grain crops, which in many instances are lying under the snow at the present time.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) as well as the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) suggested that members should not talk blue ruin. I will admit that. But they will also admit, I think, that members on the whole have stated cases exactly as they have found them in western Canada. Having lived in that province which is today leading the dominion in the production of hogs and other products, I am satisfied that any statement I have made here in connection with farming can be substantiated without any difficulty if anyone wants to take the trouble. Painting the picture as it is, is the only way to bring to the house matters as they actually are. I think that is the way to get these things rectified.
In connection with the prices of our grain, when the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke not many days -ago in the
presence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), the excuse which the minister gave for the low prices paid for grain was that there is a war on. But I would remind the minister that when he is buying munitions and other war supplies which are necessary, but no more necessary than the food which the soldiers and war workers eat, we are not told that there is a war on, because those who manufacture these articles are all paid cost plus. Why not extend the same principle to the farmers?
Then, the Minister of Agriculture told us last session that every cent which could possibly be taken out of the treasury for agriculture was being taken out; but I consider this a flimsy excuse. Why should the farmers not be treated the same as other groups in this country? They are not getting that to which, they are entitled.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is too modest to make any excuse, because he does not have one that is good enough for an hon. member from Edmonton to make.
This afternoon the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) in his address, and also the Minister of Trade and Commerce, said it was remarkable that no references were made to elimination of the Winnipeg grain exchange. If these gentlemen will read a copy of Votes and Proceedings which was distributed to-day, they will find there a notice of a bill standing in my name, which I hope will be introduced to-morrow, to amend the . Canadian Wheat Board Act. When that, is introduced they will see that all hon. members are not satisfied to. have the grain exchange operating)	
I think the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) are indebted to me for placing this notice on Votes and Proceedings, for I observe that their amendment and subamendment have been lined up directly with this, and I am glad to know that I shall have their support when this bill comes up to be discussed and voted upon.
At the present time we have very able men at the head of the wheat board. I was most sorry to learn that less than two weeks ago the third member of the board passed out of the picture, but I have every confidence in the two remaining members and in the man who I expect will be appointed in the near future. I believe, as do thousands of other farmers, that the wheat board should handle all our wheat and coarse grains.
We have been told that if the grain exchange were not in existence, we would not have benefited by the rise of price of grain which we have enjoyed during the past ten days or two weeks. In contrast to that opinion,.
Western Grain Crop

I would say that if the grain exchange, and the influence it exerts through its friends, apparently including the government, were not in existence, we would be having a far greater price at the present time and would have had' for many years past. I cannot imagine any other industry in Canada having an auction block or a gambling den to set the price of'its product, such as the grain exchange establishes to set the price of farmers' grain-. Can one imagine an insurance company putting its policies on the block and asking, "What are we offered to-day? What is offered as a premium for this policy today?" so that the price of the policy would depend mainly on the number of suckers that were in the crowd to boost or reduce the price of the premium? The same principle might apply to those who construct battleships, aeroplanes, guns and several other articles which are being used at the present time. I cannot conceive of any group being foolish enough to operate in that fashion, but because farmers are unorganized we are having this deal put over on us. Two commissions which investigated grain futures and wheat marketing in the past obtained sufficient -evidence, to show that the grain exchange [DOT]could very well be dispensed with; and as a farmer for the past twenty-nine years in western Canada*. I am quite satisfied that we can get along much better without the grain exchange than with it.
If there were sufficient time to-night, I could cite a numbeT of abuses which existed in connection with the grain trade before the wheat board was set up away back in 1919. On another occasion when we are discussing this grain situation, and particularly the closing of the grain exchange; 1 may be able to throw a little light on some of the abuses which flourished'at that time. We now have a wheat board, but I am not satisfied that such good results are being obtained as would be secured if everything were free to operate in a natural manner. The price has been artificially lifted during the past ten or twelve days. I ask, at whose expense? Whose grain was being marketed and traded to cause the price to fluctuate in the iway in which it has in the past, and who, after all, will gain the benefit? Who reaps the advantage of the rise in the price of grain and the commissions by which the farmers have been mulcted, in the trades that have been made; and who* after all, has supplied the-commissions whioh have been made by-brokers ob>
the grain exchange, the salaries which have-bees drawn-by their staffs, and other things'in-connection with this gambling den?

speechtext:
In view of certain statements which have been made, I should like to make some comments.
First, the amendment which has just been moved puts again before this parliament the position which we have taken in this chamber on numerous occasions. There is no disposition on the part of any who sit in this group to play down the possibilities of western Canada, and- particularly of the province from which we come. I want the house and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to understand that throughout the years which have gone by we have endeavoured to show the house why it was that western Canada was suffering under the disabilities from which it suffered, and to assure the people of other parts of Canada that, in spite of the dreadful years through which we passed' in the nineteen-thirties, western Canada would again produce abundantly, given one requisite, namely, sufficient moisture, sufficient min, or sufficient water.
I remember very well that in 1937, when I had the privilege of addressing a number of clubs in Ontario and other parts of Canada- Canadian clubs and so on-I thanked the people of the communities in which I spoke for the valuable assistance they had given to western Canada during our time of trial; and on every occasion I made the statement that, contrary to the opinion which was expressed in some of the newspapers and articles we were reading, western Canada would again produce in abundance.
I remember very well a statement made by the former leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, years ago, somewhat to this effect, that no similar group of people in the history of the world had produced more new wealth in a like period of time than had been produced by those who settled the western prairies. When we look around we ask ourselves, of course, where has that wealth gone? That is why we constantly urge the government and this House of Commons to see to it that the commodity which is produced in such large quantities in the prairie provinces is given a price which bears at least some relationship to the cost of production and to the prices of the articles which enter into the production of that commodity. That has been our plea all through the years, and we intend to continue to make it until there is some recognition of it.
I submit this to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and others: When we are discussing this wheat problem let us not forget that on the prairies of Canada we have produced for years within an economy

Western Grain Crop
in which the producer has had to buy his equipment and supplies at almost the highest possible price and to sell the commodity he produces in a market in competition with the same type of commodity produced under the lowest possible costs of production. The fiscal policies of all governments have militated against the region from which some of us in this house come.
I wish to say to my hon. friends to my right as well as to the government that I hope the day is not far distant when this terrible war will be over, when the world will return to a sane basis of trading, so that we may exchange commodities on a basis of equity rather than within the national financial systems and economies that have been competing against one another in the years gone by. I do not forget that it was during the regime of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when, in order that the parity of our dollar might be maintained with that of the United States and that Canada might cling to the gold standard, the western producer, as somebody said at the time, was literally nailed to a cross of gold. Wheat fell to below forty cents a bushel on the Winnipeg market. When we make a plea for adequate returns to the people who produce this vital commodity we consider that we are amply justified.
I am sorry to say that some grain is now lying in heaps on the open prairie subject to the weather and in danger of being ruined by dampness when the spring thaws come. But I believe that every kernel of this wheat will be of value in the near future. Why was it that the Minister of Agriculture was able to tell the house to-night that the price of wheat had gone up in recent days? I do not know what the answer is, but I have a suspicion. My suspicion is that there are persons going into the market to buy this wheat because they believe that it will be valuable, not only for food but for other purposes. Those who have been following the experiments being made in the manufacture of synthetic rubber and other commodities know that to a large degree the base is alcohol, and that that alcohol is being distilled from wheat.
It has been said that this year from two to three hundred million bushels of wheat will be used in the United States for the distillation of alcohol. I should like to say to the members of this house, particularly those who come from eastern Canada, that if we had a sane national economic policy at the present time, instead of building distilleries in eastern Canada and shipping back the alcohol when it is distilled, we should establish industrial
alcohol distilleries adjacent to the wheat and be prepared to manufacture in the west those articles whose base is industrial alcohol.

I am pointing out that there are possibilities for the use of grain which we have not explored. We should explore them, and we should utilize western grain to some extent for that purpose, pending the time when we shall be able once more to export our grain to feed the starving nations of the world.
I am not sold on the idea that we should continue the acreage reduction in grain this year. I think in all probability we shall find that although we had an abundant crop last year and may have a good crop this year- I quite agree with the Minister of Agriculture and I must admit that I never saw an autumn that was wetter than last year, which usually means a fair crop the following year.

There are one or two other matters to which I should like to refer. The minister placed on record the correspondence with the federation of agriculture, and I was glad to hear him read this. But that does not alter the fact that of the recommendations made by the. federation, only one has been adopted by the government, the one with reference to the 280 million bushels delivery quota for this year.

speechtext:
Yes, including the delivery of 1942 wheat on the 1943 quota. That is important. May I say to the minister that when industry is financed to the extent that it has been, some consideration ought to have been given to the provision of more storage space for grain, especially in view of the tremendous crop reaped last year. As I interjected when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) was speaking this afternoon, I know of areas in my own constituency where wheat is lying on the ground on account of the abundance of last year's yield. Unless something is done in the quite near future, this wheat will spoil. I realize the difficulty of finding storage facilities now, but I wonder whether it would not be possible to place empty cars at certain points and take the tough quota wheat at- least to the terminals where it could be dealt with and saved. Every effort should be made to save the wheat that lies on the prairies at the present time.
I say to hon. members from all parts of Canada that the prosperity of the Canadian economy depends in no small measure upon the prosperity of the prairie region. Yesterday I had a letter from a gentleman whom I know well, who has a splendid farm and is a very good farmer. He said that all his children had gone and that he could not get any hired help. He said that what distressed him most about it was that in letters he was receiving from his sons and a daughter who had gone from the .prairie region was the fact that they showed no inclination to come back; they did not want to come back to the conditions they had known, the conditions we all knew prior to the war. That is not playing down western Canada, but we must face the fact realistically if- [DOT] we want -to- continue the western wheat economy

and again I would say, what the Minister of Agriculture and others have re-[Mr. Coldwell.}	-	.	*
peated many times in this house, that over a very wide area in western Canada grain, and particularly wheat, must be the staple crop. It is true that under war conditions we are able to go into dairying, the raising of hogs and so on, but we have to face the fact that in a region which is semi-arid wheat is the cereal which will grow best and the one upon which we shall have to rely. If we are to -build up this prairie region we shall have to provide conditions of life that will give the amenities to the younger people. How that is to be done I will not discuss to-night, but I suggest that we ought to be thinking of how, when this war is over, we shall provide community life; how we shall promote cooperation among the producers so that they may escape much of the drudgery that they have known in recent years.
I suppose some of us listen occasionally to the farm and labour broadcasts. I think it was a week ago last Monday I listened to one of the labour discussion groups, when a Saskatchewan farmer from near Meadow Lake, now working in an eastern industry, recounted his experiences, and pointed out that he and his family were to-day earning every month an income half as large as the income the whole family earned in a year on the farm at Meadow Lake. Those conditions cannot continue if we want to keep this country prosperous and rebuild the prairie populations. We should be considering not only the marketing of wheat and commodity prices, but how we can bring water to the land in dry years- I believe that can be done-how we can build up the communities so that instead of the drab villages and the poor homes that so many people have had to live in although producing great wealth, we may bring to them the comforts and amenities of modern life. A great deal depends upon the price that the commodity fetches on the markets of this country and of the world.
I wish to emphasize, as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) did this afternoon,' that we are no believers in what is called inflation, but we believe that justice must be done to the worker and the farmer all across Canada. As the hon. member said this afternoon, when New Zealand is quoted to us we know quite well that there in 1936 the Labour government began a programme in which they endeavoured to bring about some parity between the farmer producing mutton, wool, cheese, butter and other agricultural products, and other industries, so that when the war broke out, they had achieved a degree of parity, not altogether satisfactory but a degree, and consequently - the government there was in a different position from our own govern-

Western Grain Crop
ment, who in a rough and ready way took a period of time when agricultural prices were low and froze them at that level.
I hope that this amendment will be supported. May I say to my hon. friends who moved the amendment to the amendment which was ruled out of order, that if they will examine the amendment moved by the hon. member for Weyburn they will find that it and the subamendment express the same point of view with the exception of the point to which Mr. Speaker objected and on the ground of which he ruled the subamendment out of order. I think this debate has served a useful purpose, and I hope that the house and the country will see to it that steps are taken to bring a measure of economic justice to the people who, as I said before, have had to buy in a most highly protected market and to sell their products on the markets of the world.

maintopic: OBJECTIVES FOR CANADIAN AGRICULTURE IN 1943
speechtext:
This
parliament has set up by statute certain bodies, the grain board and the committee on agriculture, and has enacted a grain act. It seems to me they are forgotten agencies. Why this house should seek to set up a political structure for the sale of grain or other commodities, I cannot understand. I am not surprised to see the changes which have come about in the minds of some hon. members regarding this question. It used to be said on the prairies that this industry was a free trade industry, a north and south industry and not an east and west industry for which our best customers are Great Britain and France. We saw how the free traders veered around to nine or ten different methods of protection, acreage bonus, storage bonus and many such matters. There are two or three factors, however, which have been forgotten. Two questions will have to be decided before we can lay down any price for the 1943-4 crop. One concerns the lease-lend arrangement; another, our relation with our best customer, the motherland. Are we to continue the policy of empire preferences or not? That is a most important matter. Britain is losing some of her export trade by the lease-lend arrangement. She cannot get on without exports and imports; without that trade she becomes a second Denmark, and the best days of the empire will be in the past. What is the policy of the government regarding lease-lend? What is the position of Canada in regard to the rebuilding of the devastated countries of Europe? The government of the day have not yet made up their minds. The United States, Britain and Russia know that they will have to come to the support of these countries in rebuilding, not only with food and
grain, but with building materials. These are two important matters that must first be decided.
It is the desire of every good citizen in this country that agriculture should be prosperous. We have not had that condition since confederation; we did not have it in days of peace, and it is less likely to be had in war days. The people of Ontario are very much alarmed because there is no equality of treatment in the measures passed in this country relating to the grain trade or to agriculture. One part of the country is set off against another. I am for the principle of confederation, each for all and all for each. I believe aid should be given to agriculture in all the provinces, if it is necessary; I believe aid should be given to all industries that require it, and that we should not single out the grain industry of the west. There should be equality of treatment. If agriculture on the prairies is to get help, so should agriculture in the other provinces of confederation. Many people in Ontario were greatly alarmed when a deputation came to Ottawa the other day to interview the government and present a brief in which they asked that the principal and interest of farm mortgages should be reduced, no matter when the debts were incurred and apparently without regard to ability to pay. The brief also mentioned the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. If there is one thing that has caused untold trouble in this country, it has been the political administration of that act. The principle may have been all right, but its administration has been one of the most difficult things agriculture has had to face, with debts being reduced, mortgages abandoned and all that sort of thing. Why can it not be applied to industrial workers? Hundreds and thousands of investors in Ontario invested money in mortgages in the prairies years ago. All they had to live on was the interest on their mortgages; now that interest may be wiped out in a day and their investment ruined by legislation.
If we are to have that sort of procedure, what about the industrial workers of this country; what about a brief for them? Will the government consider that, as well as the brief presented by the agricultural interests of the prairies? I say it is all wrong; there should be equality of treatment all over the country. The province of Saskatchewan is mentioned a great deal in this house. In this morning's Globe and Mail I read a long letter by Fredl Williams giving a description of the northwest field force of 1885. We talk a great deal about Saskatchewan in this house; yet We cannot get three minutes of time here
Western Grain Crop

to discuss pensions for those men, in. need now, who saved the prairie provinces and kept Canada together.
I have no doubt other opportunities will be provided to speak on these matters; but on behalf of the farmers of Ontario, British Columbia, and the maritime provinces I say that if one section of the country is to receive preferred treatment, then it will be a sorry day for the people of this country, who are now faced with a five billion dollar tax load. I plead with the government that these matters be sent to the agriculture committee and the grain board. The minister should consult with those bodies and then have the whole thing brought to the house not as a political structure but as a financial structure which the country will be able to
carry.

speechtext: No. Let us understand the situation. This is March 30, and to-morrow is March 31. We have all day to-morrow to deal with this matter; it is not necessary to pass it to-night.

war is om, but it is not necessary to rush this through. They will get their cheques, all right. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What is the undertaking that is required?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: That on some other item in the supplementaries we can discuss the cost of living bonus and how it is applied by the government. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I will undertake that that can be discussed to-morrow.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know under what item it could be discussed. There is an item for the royal mint, but that would not be very appropriate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Sunbury is asking for an undertaking that the cost of living bonus can be discussed on the supplementaries?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and I should not like to be shut off by the Chairman on the ground that the discussion was not germane to any of these items. I have looked through them hurriedly to see under what item the cost of living bonus could be discussed, but I do not see any.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: There are a number of other items in the same position as this one, ahd there is not" much advantage in putting' this' item through unless the - other salary items go through too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: To which items does the minister refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: To items 477, 421, 432, 423, 424, 425, 436, 437, 429 and 430. If the committee would put these items through tonight, it would regularize payment to-morrow. If not; if that is too big an order, we can take them up to-morrow afternoon. I do not know just what I can work out about payment. I greatly dislike any irregular or illegal payment of money. I introduced this last Friday afternoon with the expectation that it would be through before this, but we have had a debate for the last two days, and I shall just have to decide whether to let the civil servants wait or try to get the Department of Justice to advise on some way in which the obligations can be met to-morrow. The other alternative would be to put the items through to-night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: I think I understand what is in the minister's mind, but I would point out to him and to the house generally that there has grown up a practice in this house for estimates to be held back until the last unholy moment of the session, or until the last moment just before the money is required. Hon. members have not had a chance in the last three sessions, and we are now in the fourth, properly to discuss civil estimates. I put myself in the judgment of the committee if that is not a fact. Then we have the spectacle here in the dying days of a session of voting millions of dollars a minute. That is not in the public interest. I do not know just what difficulty may arise if this vote does not go through to-night, but it is in the general interests of the tax-paying public that these items should be discussed, particularly this one, which is a huge item for three-quarters of a million dollars. We also know that the allocation of the cost of living bonus is arbitrary at the hands of the treasury board. I wish to know something more about that when the time comes. I think to-morrow will be ample time to pass these items. Let us have a discussion on them to-morrow.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: Suppose somebody starts another debate on the Speaker leaving the chair?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext:
They must take the responsibility. We have not held up the discussion of these items. We did not precipitate the debate. I had no idea it would go on as loiig as it did. I hoped that we would reach these estimates to-day. We did not' do so, but' that is no reason why we should not' discuss the items. I wish to be reasonable about the matter.
Supply-Finance

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to say to the hon. member for York-Sunbury that the Minister of Finance has waited for two days to get into supply. I think everybody has been quite patient; I am not blaming anyone. But it is March 30, and it will be March 31 soon. The Minister of Finance is endeavouring now with his assistant to see if there is not some item on which the discussion which my hon. friend desires could take place so that the items can be put through to-night to regularize payment. I appreciate the consideration of the committee in waiting for a short time.. It will only be a few minutes before the minister can decide.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Could the minister
between now and to-morrow not select an item on which the cost-of-living bonus could be discussed? I appreciate the necessity of putting these items through, but like the hon. member for York-Sunbury, I consider that we should have had these estimates before us earlier. We are now faced with a situation. The civil servants ought to be paid, and I am prepared to go on and put these items through, if the minister will give an undertaking that an item can be found on which these matters can be discussed to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: That will be fair. If that can be done. I will give that undertaking if the Chair will support me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: That is the difficulty. Any member can call the attention of the Chair to the position, and the Chair must rule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: On that point may I say that I have always allowed a certain degree of latitude to meet the general desire of the committee, and I shall certainly do so again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: I would point out to the Minister of Finance and to the hon. member for York-Sunbury that the discussion could take place under item 66 in the main estimates, which is in practically the same wording.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext: We all know that, but it will be months before we reach the main- estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not said anything up to the moment, but I would say this to the minister, that we are very anxious that we or any other member of the house shall not be put in the position of withholding any proper pay from any employee of the government. I do not think any member of the house should be placed in that very unforrMb R. B. Hanson.]
tunate position, because I am quite sure that there is no hon. member who would by design do such a thing. The suggestion of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) is an impossible one, because these are supplementary estimates for the year ending to-morrow. I must say that it is very unfortunate from the minister's point of view that the particular items he is calling at the moment involve a question of gravity. The cost-of-living bonus is a matter which would normally take some time to discuss. In addition, the whole labour department is involved in a discussion of items Iftl, 422 and 423, and also the legislation items of 424 and 425, to say nothing of the others. Before we as a party will in any way give up our rights with respect to the discussion of these further supplementary estimates, we want an airtight undertaking of some description from the government that we shall have an opportunity to-morrow to discuss these items, which normally would be discussed to-night, under some other item with respect to the further supplementary estimates. I think, with that understanding, we may be able to do some business on these points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I suggest that, under item 415, "Royal Canadian Mint, including the Dominion of Canada assay office-further amount required", any of the items which I have named-417, 421, 422, 423, 424, 426, 427, 429 and 430-may be discussed to-morrow.
